scope: Professional 200 m / 400 m sprint training (100 m where it transfers). Doses and rest ratios are quoted from the sources; 'not specified in source' means the source is silent.

app_gaps.gap: Exact per-rep and per-set rest intervals for resisted sled sprint protocols: most meta-analytic sources report session volume in metres and sessions per week but not rest between reps/sets. Several entries (B-03, B-04, B-07, B-08, B-16) note the rest structure is not given rather than inventing one.

Direct dose-response comparison of 25% vs 50% vs 75% velocity-decrement sled loads on the same outcome measure: PMC11469994 reports subgroup effect sizes by Vdec but no significant between-load comparison was verifiable from the fetched text.

A live primary source for the Saez de Villarreal plyometric meta-analysis full text (only the PubMed abstract was retrievable); per-study contact counts and rest intervals for that meta-analysis could not be verified.

Motorised-resistance (1080 Sprint) assisted-sprint chronic training studies with full set/rep/rest prescriptions - only a reliability study (Frontiers 2025, 3 kg load, 21 participants) and a coach roundtable were fetched; the chronic dosing was not verifiable.

Contrast/complex training rest intervals prescribed specifically for sprint (rather than jump) outcomes: the PAP review and French contrast meta-analysis give intra-complex rest indirectly (7-8 min, 4-8 min), but no fetched source gave a sprint-specific contrast session with both inter-set and intra-complex rest stated.
No fetched source gave absolute 1RM/body-mass benchmark bands for elite 100/200/400 m sprinters specifically - the McBride and Wisloff evidence is from football/soccer cohorts.

Incline/hill sprint chronic training studies with full sets x reps x rest for sprinters (the uphill-running meta-analysis located is in middle-distance/recreational cohorts and its pooled effects on strength and jump were non-significant).

field: individual_maximal_lactate_and_lactate_curve; why_not_in_research: Published studies report group means; a lactate curve is athlete- and protocol-specific. The app must capture post-effort lactate values and the test speed/load at which they were taken.

field: session_rpe_and_load_history; why_not_in_research: sRPE is an athlete-reported product (RPE × duration); no publication contains this athlete's history. Needed to time tapers and flag non-functional overreaching.

field: caffeine_responder_status; why_not_in_research: CYP1A2/ADORA2A genotype and habitual intake are individual; the literature reports contradictory 3 vs 6-9 mg/kg outcomes. Ask the athlete for habitual dose, response and side effects.

field: individual_supplement_tolerance_and_GI_history; why_not_in_research: Sodium bicarbonate and nitrate effects are dominated by individual GI tolerance/responder status; trials report group averages only.
field: individual_taper_response; why_not_in_research: Taper length in elite practice ranges from 10 to 30 days with wide individual variation; no study gives a per-athlete value.

field: personal_best_and_split_history; why_not_in_research: All published prediction rules (Mike Smith doubling +10%, Dick 1987 controls, flying-30 → 100 m) are population or elite-descriptive rules; the app needs the athlete's own legal PBs, wind readings, and 100/200/300/400 m splits to fit a personal model.

field: electronic_timing_setup_and_calibration_log; why_not_in_research: Hand-vs-gate offsets vary with setup (0.15-0.20 s is a literature estimate). The app needs the athlete's own paired hand/gate data to establish the correction.

field: menstrual_cycle_phase_and_hormonal_contraceptive_status; why_not_in_research: Nitrate studies under-represent female participants and no sex-specific dosing guidelines exist (stated in the 2025 nitrate meta-analysis). Phase data must be asked for.

field: sleep_and_circadian_testing_time; why_not_in_research: Maximal velocity varies by time of day; the literature only says 'test at the same time'. The app must record actual sleep and session clock times.

field: nutrition_intake_and_energy_availability; why_not_in_research: Energy availability has no field measurement; blood/urine markers are lab-only. Requires athlete food logs, body mass and training load.

field: psychological_baseline_scores; why_not_in_research: CSAI-2/SCAT/FFMQ baseline values are per-athlete questionnaire outputs; studies report only group changes. The app must administer the instrument.

field: right_left_hamstring_strength_asymmetry; why_not_in_research: Nordic break-angle/force values and asymmetry norms were not extractable from the sources fetched; requires the athlete's own bilateral measurements.

field: individual_recovery_time_between_heats; why_not_in_research: No published protocol exists for the short between-heats window in 200/400 m competition; the app must log the athlete's actual gap, intake and performance by round.

field: equipment_and_surface_conditions; why_not_in_research: Spike model, track surface, wind, temperature and altitude materially change sprint times but are recorded ad hoc in the literature — must be captured per session.

protocols.title: Speed Endurance Training (SET): definition, scope and mechanisms - Bangsbo, Kissow & Hostrup 2025
protocols.protocol: SET is defined by the review as 'exercise training performed at intensities higher than that eliciting maximum oxygen uptake (VO2-max)' - i.e. exercise above 80% of all exercise intensities for most individuals (verbatim: 'for most individuals, SET encounters more than 80% of all exercise intensities'). | The review covers events lasting 20-60 s (400-m run ~43 s men / ~48 s women; 400-m hurdles ~45 s / ~51 s; 200-m sprint canoeing ~38 s / ~45 s; 500-m speed skating ~34 s / ~36 s; 500-m cycling TT ~29 s / ~33 s), 1-10 min (800/1500 m, 4-min track cycling, 2000-m rowing), 10-60 min, and repeated-intense sport. | Core claim: 'SET enhances performance across all event durations, even when training volume is markedly reduced.' | Mechanism claim: 'The performance enhancements arise despite no changes in VO2-max and are typically associated with improved exercise economy and a greater capacity to handle muscle ionic shifts and counter exercise-induced reductions in pH.' | Standard test outcomes used for 10-60 s events: running distance in 30 s, time of a 200-m run, or mean power in a 30-s Wingate test. | Inclusion criterion: only trained/well-trained/athlete subjects with VO2-max >45 mL/kg/min (female) and >50 mL/kg/min (male). | Documented adaptations across the reviewed trials: MCT1 +50%, Na+-K+ ATPase subunit alpha1 +29%, alpha2 +36%, beta1 +15%, NHE1 +30-75%, buffering capacity +44%, SERCA II +20%, CS +11%, PFK +23-30%, phosphorylase activity +40%, MHCIIa +19%.
protocols.dose: Training interventions reviewed are catalogued in Table 1 with exact sets/reps/work/rest/frequency and %-volume change per study - see entry A02 for the running-based doses. | Volume reductions as large as -64% (Iaia 2008), -58% (Vorup 2016) and -38% (Skovgaard 2017) accompanied performance improvement.
dose_raw: Training interventions reviewed are catalogued in Table 1 with exact sets/reps/work/rest/frequency and %-volume change per study - see entry A02 for the running-based doses.
Volume reductions as large as -64% (Iaia 2008), -58% (Vorup 2016) and -38% (Skovgaard 2017) accompanied performance improvement.
protocols.rest_ratio: Rest between SET bouts varies by study and is tabulated in Table 1 (see A02 for exact values); the review's own examples: 30-s intervals separated by 3 min (SET-P) and 1-min intervals separated by 1 min (SET-M).
protocols.app_rule: Primary peer-reviewed anchor for defining 'speed endurance' as a physiological construct (supra-VO2max intensity) rather than a coach category. Explicit that SET works even when total volume is cut sharply - directly relevant to the 200 m and 400 m taper/competition phases.
protocols.caveats: Narrative review, not a meta-analysis: study selection is author-driven; no pooled effect size is reported. | Most interventions used running or cycling, 'and not all studies used a sport-specific field test'; the review notes some sport-specific training studies (e.g. Papandreou et al.) were excluded by its VO2-max inclusion filter. | No 200-m-track-specific intervention appears in the review's tables - the 200 m is reported only via the Iaia football study (200-m run improved 2%) and 30-s tests.

protocols.title: Exact speed-endurance protocols and doses reported by the SET review; SET-P vs SET-M
protocols.protocol: SET is split into two sub-modes by the review: 'production training' (SET-P) = 'high anaerobic, primarily glycolytic, ATP turnover during repeated short intervals (10-40 s) with relatively long recovery periods, for example, 30-s intervals separated by 3 min of recovery'; and 'maintenance training' (SET-M) = 'exercise periods lasting 5-120 s with shorter recovery periods to develop fatigue during repeated bouts, for example, 1-min intervals separated by 1 min of recovery, thereby increasing exercise tolerance.' | Running-based SET (Table 1, doses verbatim): Bickham et al. 2006 - 7 M runners, 6 weeks of 14-30 x 40-100 m near-maximal sprint at 90-100%, 5 min rest, 3/week; outcomes: intense exercise (~2.5 min) +11%, Type II fibres +6%, MCT1 +50%. | Dawson et al. 1998 - 9 M trained, 6 weeks of 3-5 sets of 4-8 x 40-100 m near-maximal sprint at 90-100%, 2-4 min rest between reps, 3/week; outcomes: repeated sprint +2%, intense exercise (~1 min) +11%, phosphorylase activity +40%, CS activity -36%. | Vorup et al. 2016 - 16 M runners, 8 weeks of 4-8 x 30-s all-out, 3 min rest, 2/week plus resistance/moderate/high-intensity aerobic training 2/week, total training volume -58%; 400-m running (~1 min) +5%, Yo-Yo 2 +19%. | Iaia et al. 2008 - 4 weeks of 8-12 x 30-s all-out, 3 min rest, 3-4/week, volume -64%; 30-s all-out +7%, Yo-Yo 2 +19%, intense exercise (~1.5 min) +27%. | Iaia et al. (football, cited in the discussion) - 5 weeks of 1-3 sets of 6 x 5-s sprints with 15-s rest, 1-2/week; 200-m run performance improved 2%. | Skovgaard et al. 2018 - 40 days of 10 SET sessions of 5-10 x 30-s all-out with 3.5 min rest plus 10 AMI sessions, volume -36%; 10 km (~45-48 min) +1.7%. | Hov et al. 2022 - SET-P: 8 weeks of 10 x 30-s all-out, 3.5 min active rest, 3/week vs SET-M: 8 weeks of ~8 x 20-s all-out with 10-s passive rest aiming to exhaust the subject during the 8th or 9th interval, 3/week; SET-M improved 3-km +4.1% and 300-m sprint (~45 s) +4.4% vs SET-P +2.2% and +3.3%. | Nevill et al. 1989 - 8 weeks of 2 x 30-s all-out (10 min rest) + 6-10 x 6-s all-out (54-s rest) + 2-5 x 2-min all-out (5 min rest), 3-4/week; 30-s all-out +6%, anaerobic glycolytic ATP production rate +14%, in vivo buffering capacity +44%. | Skovgaard et al. 2017 - FAM: 40 days of 10 SET sessions of 10 x 30-s all-out, 3.5 min rest plus 10 AMI sessions, volume -32% to -38%; HF: 40 days of 20 SET sessions of 8-12 x 30-s all-out, 3.5 min rest plus 20 AMI, volume -38%.
protocols.dose: Running SET, single-set form: 14-30 x 40-100 m at 90-100%, 5 min rest, 3/wk, 6 wk (Bickham 2006). | Running SET, multiple-set form: 3-5 sets x (4-8 x 40-100 m) at 90-100%, 2-4 min rest between reps, 3/wk, 6 wk (Dawson 1998) - this is the canonical '4-6 x 150 m'-type dose family. | Time-based SET for 400-m-equivalent durations: 4-8 x 30-s all-out, 3 min rest, 2/wk, 8 wk (Vorup 2016); 8-12 x 30-s all-out, 3 min rest, 3-4/wk, 4 wk (Iaia 2008); 10-12 x 30-s all-out, 4.5 min rest, 2-3/wk, 7 wk (Gunnarsson 2013). | Short-rep form supporting 200 m: 1-3 sets x 6 x 5-s sprints, 15-s rest, 1-2/wk, 5 wk (Iaia, football).
dose_raw: Running SET, single-set form: 14-30 x 40-100 m at 90-100%, 5 min rest, 3/wk, 6 wk (Bickham 2006).
Running SET, multiple-set form: 3-5 sets x (4-8 x 40-100 m) at 90-100%, 2-4 min rest between reps, 3/wk, 6 wk (Dawson 1998) - this is the canonical '4-6 x 150 m'-type dose family.

Time-based SET for 400-m-equivalent durations: 4-8 x 30-s all-out, 3 min rest, 2/wk, 8 wk (Vorup 2016); 8-12 x 30-s all-out, 3 min rest, 3-4/wk, 4 wk (Iaia 2008); 10-12 x 30-s all-out, 4.5 min rest, 2-3/wk, 7 wk (Gunnarsson 2013).
Short-rep form supporting 200 m: 1-3 sets x 6 x 5-s sprints, 15-s rest, 1-2/wk, 5 wk (Iaia, football).
protocols.rest_ratio: Between SET-P reps: 3 min (Iaia 2008, Vorup 2016), 3.5 min (Skovgaard, Hov), 4.5 min (Gunnarsson 2013), 5 min (Bickham 2006). | Between running reps within a set: 2-4 min (Dawson 1998). | SET-M short-recovery variant: 10-s passive rest between 20-s bouts (Hov 2022); 15-s rest between 5-s sprints (Iaia). | The review's stated rationale: SET-P's 'relatively long recovery periods' preserve glycolytic ATP turnover per bout, whereas SET-M's short recovery is used 'to develop fatigue during repeated bouts... thereby increasing exercise tolerance'.
protocols.app_rule: Gives the exact numeric doses the review reports for speed-endurance work and formalises the distinction a 400 m coach needs: SET-P (glycolytic production, long rest) vs SET-M (fatigue tolerance, short rest).
protocols.caveats: No protocol in Table 1 is a 200 m or 400 m track-sprint study; the running studies used 30-s all-out or 40-100 m sprints with 400-m-run / Yo-Yo / repeated-sprint outcomes. Do not relabel these as 200 m/400 m prescriptions. | The '3x4x60 m' and '2x200 m' dose shapes commonly quoted from coach literature do NOT appear in this review - they come from coach practice sources (see A12, A15). 'not specified in source' for those exact shapes here.

protocols.title: Energy-system contribution to 200 m and 400 m: aerobic vs anaerobic, PCr vs glycolysis, O2 deficit
protocols.protocol: Crossover (systematic review, 102 studies / 311 data points; O2-deficit method in 66 studies): maximal duration at which anaerobic and aerobic contributions are EQUAL = 78.6 s (95% CI +/-1.1 s). Anaerobic predominance holds up to ~75-80 s. No difference between running and cycling, or by training status; small but significant effects of measurement method and pacing strategy. | 200 m (Briand 2025 model, men): total energy 1171 J/kg = 20% alactic (PCr) / 67% lactic (glycolysis) / 12% aerobic. Women's 200 m: 17 / 69 / 14. Anaerobic:aerobic = 88/12 men, 86/14 women. | 400 m (Briand 2025 model, men): total energy 1925 J/kg (observed 1942 J/kg) = 9% alactic (170 J/kg) / 62% lactic (1189 J/kg) / 29% aerobic (566 J/kg). Women's 400 m: 8 / 62 / 31 (144 / 1155 / 571 J/kg of 1870). Anaerobic:aerobic = 70/30 men, 69/31 women. | 100 m for comparison (Briand 2025): 47% alactic / 48% lactic / 5% aerobic (men); 37 / 56 / 7 (women). | Maximal capacities in the model: alactic 376 J/kg male / 259 J/kg female; lactic 1314 J/kg male / 1194 J/kg female. Theoretical alactic range 310-390 J/kg (men), 230-292 (women). | Substrate accounting: rest PCr ~20 mmol/kg and ATP ~6 mmol/kg fresh muscle; usable PCr ~20 mmol/kg active muscle = 4-5 mmol/kg body mass, giving PCr energy 310-390 J/kg. Glycolytic power peaks at ~6 s; glycolytic decay time constant ~30 s; max glycolytic rate ~1 mmol/L/s lactate. 400 m blood lactate 15-20 mmol/L above rest, up to 25 mmol/L. | Acceleration cost as a share of total energy: 36% (100 m), 22% (200 m), 10% (400 m). | Spencer & Gastin 2001 (20 national-standard athletes; 200 m n=3, 400 m n=6, 800 m n=5, 1500 m n=6): aerobic contribution 200 m 29+/-4%, 400 m 43+/-1%, 800 m 66+/-2%, 1500 m 84+/-1%. AOD: 200 m 30.4+/-2.3, 400 m 41.3+/-1.0, 800 m 48.1+/-4.5, 1500 m 47.1+/-3.8 mL/kg. Crossover to predominantly aerobic stated as 'between 15 and 30 s'. | Documented disagreement in the 400 m aerobic estimate (Arcelli et al., New Studies in Athletics 23(2):15-23, 2008, table of prior claims): Lacour 1990 = 28% aerobic; Newsholme 1992 = 25%; Foss & Keteyian 1998 = 18%; Nummela & Rusko 1995 and Hill 1999 = minimum 37%; Duffield 2005 = 41% men / 45% women; Weyand 1994 = 64-70%. Their own derived pattern: aerobic contribution 24% at 44 s, 33% at 48 s, 43% at 52 s.
protocols.dose: not specified in source (these are measurement/modelling studies, not training interventions)
dose_raw: not specified in source (these are measurement/modelling studies, not training interventions)
protocols.app_rule: Defines the bioenergetic target: the 200 m is ~86-88% anaerobic and the 400 m ~69-70% anaerobic by model, with the anaerobic/aerobic crossover at 78.6 s - so both events sit in the anaerobic-dominant zone and the 400 m is the last event at which anaerobic still predominates.
protocols.caveats: The Briand 2025 split is MODEL output fitted to world-record velocity profiles, not direct muscle measurement - treat the 9/62/29 split as a model estimate. | The literature genuinely disagrees on the 400 m aerobic fraction (18% to 70% across cited sources); the spread is partly method-driven (AOD vs La/PCr vs theoretical models), which the systematic review confirms as a significant method effect. | Spencer & Gastin used n=3 for the 200 m - the 29% figure for the 200 m rests on three athletes.

protocols.title: In-race 400 m and 800 m energy contribution, race VO2, oxygen deficit and blood lactate - Duffield, Dawson & Goodman 2005
protocols.protocol: Subjects: 16 trained 400 m runners (11 M, 5 F) and 11 trained 800 m runners; 400 m group race time 52.2+/-1.9 s (men), 60.2+/-4.1 s (women). | 400 m contribution by AOD method: men 41.3+/-10.9% aerobic / 58.7+/-10.9% anaerobic (range 31-60% / 40-69%); women 44.5+/-7.6% / 55.5+/-7.6%. | 400 m contribution by La/PCr method (same athletes): men 35.2+/-7.1% aerobic / 64.8+/-7.1% anaerobic (26-45% / 55-74%); women 37.0+/-6.2% / 63.0+/-6.2%. | 800 m (AOD): 60.3+/-9.0% aerobic (men), 70.1+/-16.2% (women). | 400 m men in-race physiology: peak race VO2 49.22+/-10.39 mL/kg/min = 81.6+/-8.1% of peak VO2; peak race HR 187+/-7 bpm (97+/-3% HRmax); peak blood lactate 13.9+/-2.3 mmol/L; race AOD 48.0+/-14.8 mL O2 eq/kg; total energy cost 0.205+/-0.027 mL O2/kg/m; mean speed 7.68+/-0.28 m/s. | 400 m women: peak VO2 42.70+/-7.38 mL/kg/min (81.6+/-3.2% of peak VO2); peak lactate 13.3+/-2.9 mmol/L; race AOD 41.8+/-10.5 mL O2 eq/kg. | PCr store contribution in their La/PCr model = 37.0 mL O2/kg muscle mass. | Negative correlations between anaerobic (La/PCr) contribution and performance: r = -0.77 (male 800 m), r = -0.87 (female 400 m), p<0.05. | Their literature table: anaerobic estimates for the 400 m range from 36% to 72%; the only prior female value was 62% (Hill 1999); their conclusion is ~60% anaerobic.
protocols.dose: not specified in source (physiological measurement study, no training prescription)
dose_raw: not specified in source (physiological measurement study, no training prescription)
protocols.app_rule: The best direct in-race 400 m dataset for the aerobic/anaerobic split computed two ways, plus actual peak race VO2 (~82% of VO2max) and peak blood lactate (~14 mmol/L) values.
protocols.caveats: Group mean race time 52.2 s (men) is sub-elite; elite 400 m runners run ~43-45 s, so absolute VO2 and lactate values will differ at elite speed. | The two methods disagree by ~6 percentage points of aerobic contribution within the same athletes; AOD vs La/PCr is the single biggest methodological lever on this number.

protocols.title: Measured VO2, acid-base balance and segmental anaerobic contribution in a maximal 400 m - Vilmi et al. 2016
protocols.protocol: Adults (n=8) ran a maximal 400 m; anaerobic (AOD) contribution 53+/-5% in adults vs 44+/-7% in adolescents (P<0.05) and 45+/-5% in children (P<0.05). | Segmental anaerobic contribution across the adult 400 m: 75+/-6% (first 100 m), 55+/-5% (second 100 m), 40+/-6% (third 100 m), 41+/-5% (final 100 m). | VO2peak during the 400 m = 60.7+/-2.4 mL/kg/min in adults = 101+/-10% of their VO2max test value. | Adult VO2 fell from 59.7+/-4.0 mL/kg/min at 30-35 s to 55.3+/-4.4 mL/kg/min at 45-50 s (P<0.001) - VO2 declines at the end of a 400 m despite sustained effort. | Nadir blood pH: adults 6.97+/-0.06, adolescents 7.14+/-0.07, children 7.18+/-0.03. Lowest individual adult pH 6.87. | Peak blood lactate: adults 17.4+/-1.8 mmol/L (highest individual 20.2), adolescents 13.3+/-3.7, children 10.2+/-1.1. | Their literature framing states total anaerobic contribution is 57-65% and 'might be even as great as 75% in top level athletes', with a quoted breakdown of 'PCr 10%, anaerobic glycolysis 50% and oxygen uptake 40%' and VO2peak during a 400 m typically 80-95% of VO2max.
protocols.dose: not specified in source
dose_raw: not specified in source
protocols.app_rule: Provides the segmental picture a 400 m coach needs: the first 100 m is ~75% anaerobic while the final three 100 m segments sit at ~40-55% - the physiological reason the last 100 m cannot be run as fast as the first.
protocols.caveats: Small n (8 adults); the adults' 400 m times were not elite. | The segmental percentages are the source's own derived values and sum to a whole-race estimate of ~53% anaerobic, which is internally consistent but not directly measured per segment.

protocols.title: 400 m VO2 kinetics and why VO2 falls late in the race - Hanon et al.
protocols.protocol: Hanon 2010 (10 trained runners, outdoor track): peak VO2 during the 400 m = 93.9+/-3.9% of VO2max, reached at 24.4+/-3.2 s (i.e. ~192+/-22 m). | A significant VO2 decrease occurred in the last 100 m (P<0.05) even while velocity stayed above v-VO2max. | VO2 in the final 5 s correlated with blood pH at 300 m r = 0.86 (P<0.0005) and with [HCO3-] r = 0.70 (P<0.05). | Velocity decrease in the last 100 m correlated with [HCO3-] r = -0.83 (P<0.001) and with pH r = -0.69 (P<0.05) - the more acidosis, the bigger the late-race speed loss. | Hanon & Thomas 2011: VO2peak as % of VO2max = 94% (400 m), 100% (800 and 1500 m); final-100 m velocity = 77% of 400 m peak velocity (vs 88% for 800 m, 96% for 1500 m). | VO2 decrease over the last 100 m = 15.6+/-6.5% (400 m), 9.9+/-6.3% (800 m), 3.6+/-7.6% (1500 m); the amplitude of that decrease correlated with tidal-volume reduction r = 0.85 (P<0.0001) and peak blood lactate r = 0.55 (P<0.005). | Mechanistic discussion (Hanon 2013, SpringerPlus 2:651): the VO2 drop is proportionally larger than the velocity drop; cites 'VO2 decreases by 2% for each 1% decrease of SaO2' (Harms et al. 2000).
protocols.dose: not specified in source
dose_raw: not specified in source
protocols.app_rule: Quantifies the 400 m's late-race collapse: the final 100 m is run at ~77% of peak velocity with a 15.6% fall in VO2, and both trace back to acidosis - the mechanistic case for why a 400 m cannot be evenly paced and why tolerating H+ accumulation is the trainable quality.
protocols.caveats: n=10 (2010) and a within-subject design (2011) - small-sample and non-elite; group 400 m times were not elite. | Correlations are associative; no causal intervention is reported.

protocols.title: Anaerobic capacity (MAOD) in sprinters vs other event groups, and its link to 100/400 m performance
protocols.protocol: Scott et al. 1991: MAOD values by event group - sprinters 78, middle-distance 74, distance runners 56, controls 56 mL O2 eq/kg (P<=0.05). Relative anaerobic contribution during 2-3 min runs at 125-140% VO2max = 39% (sprinters), 37% (middle-distance), 30% (distance, P<=0.05). | Ramsbottom et al. 1994: mean AOD 66.1+/-12.0 mL O2 eq/kg; O2 deficit 22.8+/-8.2 mL/kg/min at test intensity 117.4+/-11.4% VO2max (range 105-144%); mean track times 13.6+/-1.3 s (100 m), 60.9+/-6.8 s (400 m), 138.8+/-18.5 s (800 m). | Ramsbottom 1994 correlations: AOD vs performance r = -0.88 (100 m), -0.82 (400 m), -0.61 (800 m); VO2max vs 400 m r = 0.78. Trial-to-trial AOD reproducibility 65.2+/-10.9 vs 66.3+/-12.5 mL O2 eq/kg (r = 0.94). | Olesen et al. 1994: total anaerobic energy release computed from rest lactate 2 mmol/kg wet, CP 20 mmol/kg wet, ATP decrease 2 mmol/kg wet - approximately 36 mmol ATP/kg wet muscle (25% active muscle mass, 6.5 mol ATP per mol O2). Maximal O2 deficit (MOD) is larger in 400 m runners than untrained and rises until exercise exceeds 2 min.
protocols.dose: not specified in source (test protocols, not training prescriptions)
dose_raw: not specified in source (test protocols, not training prescriptions)
protocols.app_rule: Establishes that anaerobic capacity (a) discriminates sprinters from other groups, (b) is highly correlated with 100 m and 400 m performance (r = -0.88 / -0.82), and (c) is reliably measurable (r = 0.94 trial-to-trial).
protocols.caveats: MAOD/AOD methods were not standardised across these studies (oxygen deficit vs maximal accumulated oxygen deficit), which limits pooling. | Scott 1991's relative-contribution figures come from 2-3 min runs, not sprints - the 39%-vs-30% sprinter/distance gap is directionally useful but is not a 400 m number.

protocols.title: Post-competition blood lactate after 400 m and 800 m races and its relation to performance - Lacour et al. 1990
protocols.protocol: 17 top-level runners measured after real competition; mean post-competition blood lactate 20.8 mmol/L (SD 2.34). | Race distance had no effect on post-race lactate: 21.1+/-3.56 mmol/L (male) vs 20.1+/-2.38 mmol/L (female). | Highest single recorded value 27 mmol/L (a female athlete). | Blood lactate vs relative 400 m performance: r = 0.85 (males, P<0.01), r = 0.80 (females, P<0.05). | Assumptions used in their calculations: VO2-uptake time constant 30 s; muscle high-energy phosphate decrease 18 mmol/kg wet; 1 mmol/L lactate rise = 3.30 mL O2/kg.

dose_raw: not specified in source
protocols.app_rule: Anchors the realistic post-400 m blood lactate ceiling (~21 mmol/L mean, 27 mmol/L max) that 400 m speed-endurance work habituates the athlete to, and shows lactate rises track performance within the event.
protocols.caveats: Author list is not printed on the fetched page; attribution to 'Lacour et al.' follows the IAAF New Studies in Athletics paper fetched in the same lane, which cites 'LACOUR et al. (1990)' for 400 m aerobic = 28%. | Post-race peripheral lactate is an index, not a measure of muscle anaerobic ATP turnover; the r = 0.85 correlation is not causal.

protocols.title: Blood lactate dynamics: 350 m vs 500 m trials as competing special-endurance stimuli for the 400 m
protocols.protocol: Design: 11 elite male 400 m sprinters split into a 350 m group (n=6) and a 500 m group (n=5); plasma lactate measured before start, after warm-up, immediately before the test, and at 1, 3, 12, 20 and 40 min post-exercise (enzymatic Sentinel test, Italy). | Blood lactate concentration differed between groups, reaching statistical significance at the 3 min post-exercise time point; no significant differences at the other time points. | The 350 m trial produced higher peak lactate, indicating a greater acute anaerobic demand. | The 500 m trial required a longer recovery period for lactate clearance and return to homeostasis. | Authors' framing: the study aimed to identify which distance 'may more effectively develop special endurance for the 400 m run'.
protocols.dose: Test distances: 350 m and 500 m maximal trials. No training prescription is reported in the abstract.
dose_raw: Test distances: 350 m and 500 m maximal trials. No training prescription is reported in the abstract.
protocols.rest_ratio: Blood-sampling time points: pre-start, post-warm-up, pre-test, and 1 / 3 / 12 / 20 / 40 min post-exercise. The 500 m trial required longer for lactate clearance; the exact clearance half-time is 'not specified in source'.
protocols.app_rule: Directly addresses the 400 m coach's practical fork between 350 m and 500 m special-endurance reps: 350 m maximises acute anaerobic demand, 500 m extends the clearance/recovery demand.
protocols.caveats: FULL TEXT NOT RETRIEVED - direct MDPI access was blocked from this network; only the abstract and metadata were obtained (via the DOAJ REST API). No effect sizes, no exact mmol/L values, no p-values beyond 'significant at 3 min', and no training doses are available. | n=11 total, split 6/5 - very small; 'elite male 400 m sprinters' is the authors' description of the sample. | Treat as abstract-level evidence only; do not cite specific mmol/L figures from it.

protocols.title: Phosphocreatine resynthesis half-times and recovery kinetics - the physiological basis of rest-interval length
protocols.protocol: Harris et al. 1976 (quadriceps biopsies after exercise to fatigue, PC down to ~15% of rest): BIPHASIC resynthesis with a FAST component half-time of 21 s after dynamic exercise and 22.5 s after isometric exercise, and a SLOW component half-time >170 s in both cases. The paper warns that a single half-time fitted across the whole deficit lands between those extremes depending on the sampling window. No resynthesis at all when circulation is occluded. | Fast component of O2-debt repayment: half-time ~25 s (Margaria, as reported in Harris 1976). | Bogdanis et al. 1995 (30 s all-out cycling, biopsies at 1.5/3/6 min): end-of-sprint PCr 19.7+/-1.2% and ATP 70.5+/-6.5% of rest; muscle lactate 119.0+/-4.6 mmol/kg dry wt; pH 6.72+/-0.06. | Bogdanis 1995 recovery: PCr back to 65.0+/-2.8% of rest at 1.5 min and only 85.5+/-3.5% at 6 min. Average half-time for PCr resynthesis = 56.6+/-7.3 s (power-function fit). Peak power, peak pedal speed and 0-6 s mean power had NOT recovered after 6 min. | Bogdanis 1995: percentage PCr resynthesis correlated with percentage power restoration at 1.5 and 3 min, r = 0.71-0.86 (P<0.05); no relation between pH recovery and power restoration (P>0.05). | Bogdanis et al. 1996 (two 30-s sprints 4 min apart): after 3.8 min recovery pH was still 6.80+/-0.03 while PCr had resynthesised to 78.7+/-3.3% of rest. PCr resynthesis % vs power recovery in the first 10 s of sprint 2: r = 0.84 and r = 0.91. Anaerobic ATP turnover fell from 235+/-9 to 139+/-7 mmol/kg dry muscle (glycolysis down ~45%) while work in sprint 2 fell only ~18%; aerobic metabolism supplied ~49% of the energy in sprint 2. | Singh et al. 2025 meta-analysis (128 studies, 31P-MRS): pooled PCr recovery time constants - forearm 34.41 s (SD 17), upper leg 35.66 s (SD 9), lower leg 33.75 s (SD 10); before outlier removal lower leg 37.73 s (SD 15). Pooled mean difference diseased vs control 15.96 s (95% CI 1.70-30.22, p=0.03). Older age and more acidic end-exercise pH extend recovery (r = -0.726 between lower end-exercise pH and recovery rate in healthy subjects). | McMahon & Jenkins 2002 (review): PCr can fall below 40% of resting concentration within 10 s of intense exercise; fatigue/power recovery half-time ~32 s.
protocols.dose: not specified in source
dose_raw: not specified in source
protocols.rest_ratio: Practical mapping implied by the kinetics: ~21-22 s half-time for the fast PCr component (Harris 1976), a 56.6 s average half-time after a 30-s all-out sprint (Bogdanis 1995), and full restoration that 'can take as long as 3 min' (Rogers et al. 2024, see A11). | Bogdanis 1996: after 3.8 min rest PCr was 78.7% restored - the measured basis for the 3-5 min rest used in repeated ~30-s speed-endurance sets.
protocols.app_rule: The 'why' behind every rest interval in a 400 m programme: brief rests (<60 s) leave PCr low and force glycolytic/aerobic supply; long rests (>3-4 min) allow near-complete PCr restoration, which is what selects for maximal-quality reps.
protocols.caveats: The 21 s (Harris 1976) and 56.6 s (Bogdanis 1995) half-times differ because of exercise modality, depletion depth and fit window - quoting either as 'THE' PCr half-time is wrong; both are reported in the fetched sources. | Singh 2025's pooled constants come mostly from submaximal/intense (not all-out sprint) protocols and are post-exercise recovery time constants, not pure PCr half-times.

protocols.title: Rest length selects the training stimulus: RSA / SIT / IST work-to-rest categories and the PCr restoration window
protocols.protocol: Work-to-rest classification (Rogers 2024, introduction synthesis): partial PCr recovery occurs during the first ~22 s and full restoration can take as long as 3 min. | RSA (repeated-sprint ability) = efforts of 3-7 s with INCOMPLETE rest of <60 s. SIT (sprint interval training) = 20-30 s efforts with 2-4 min recovery and elevated blood lactate. IST (intermittent sprint training) = efforts <10 s with rest >60 s allowing greater/near-complete recovery. | Stimulus selection: IST 'targets phosphagen development'; RSA 'necessarily involves glycogen and aerobic contribution' - rest length, not rep distance, is what changes the system trained. | Mendez-Villanueva 2012 (5 x 6-s all-out sprints, 30-s recovery, extended to 11 sprints): 30-s recovery intervals were 'sufficient to allow significant PCr resynthesis'; PCr resynthesis over 6 min correlated with work in sprint 11, r = 0.79, and with the last five sprints, r = 0.67 (P<0.05). | Critically: muscle pH stayed depressed with NO correlation to performance recovery - PCr resynthesis, not pH, tracked performance recovery across repeated sprints.
protocols.dose: The sources' own intervention doses: 5 x 6-s all-out with 30-s recovery (Mendez-Villanueva 2012); the RSA/SIT/IST categories map to 3-7 s with <60 s rest, 20-30 s with 2-4 min recovery, and <10 s with >60 s rest respectively (Rogers 2024).
dose_raw: The sources' own intervention doses: 5 x 6-s all-out with 30-s recovery (Mendez-Villanueva 2012); the RSA/SIT/IST categories map to 3-7 s with <60 s rest, 20-30 s with 2-4 min recovery, and <10 s with >60 s rest respectively (Rogers 2024).
protocols.rest_ratio: Operative rule derived from these sources: rest <60 s is too short for meaningful PCr restoration and selects for glycolytic/aerobic supply and lactate accumulation; 2-4 min is the SIT/speed-endurance band; the first ~22 s recovers PCr only partially and full restoration can take up to 3 min. | Measured check: 30-s rest gives significant (but incomplete) PCr resynthesis, not full recovery (Mendez-Villanueva 2012).
protocols.app_rule: Turns 'how long do I rest?' into a system-selection decision: to train the 400 m's glycolytic capacity you deliberately choose incomplete rest; to train maximal quality you choose the 3-4 min band.
protocols.caveats: Rogers 2024's category definitions and the ~22 s / 3 min figures come from its introduction's synthesis of cited work, not from its own trial. | Mendez-Villanueva used 5-6 s cycling sprints, not track reps of 150-300 m; the principle transfers but the exact rest values do not scale linearly.

protocols.title: Rest intervals and doses actually used in published 400 m coach programmes (Anderson, Troy Johnson)
protocols.protocol: Vince Anderson (USTFCCCA 2023): alactic short endurance prescribed as 3-4 sets x (2 x 50 m) at ~90% with 1 min between reps and 2 min between sets; absolute speed 6 x 45 m maximal with 3-4 min between reps; intensive tempo 3 x 300 m with 8 min, or 2 x 250 m with 6 min; special endurance 1 as 5 x 200 m with 5 min, or a 350/250/150 ladder with 10-12 min and 6-8 min. | Troy Johnson (2014 SuperClinic, USATF Level III) - speed endurance (ATP/glycolytic) listed verbatim as '4-6x150m 4-7min rest', '2x3x200 5min/10min sets w/recovery jog', '6-10x200 3min'; special endurance (glycolytic) as '4-6x300m 7-10 min rest' and '6-10x200m 3-5 min rest'; lactate threshold as '3x300m w/7 min rest'; lactate capacity as '3x350m w/full recovery'. His ATP-CP work: flying 20/30/40 m, block starts 5-10 x 10 m and 5-10 x 20 m, and 'Sprints <80m rest for 1 set/3-4min'.
protocols.dose: Anderson: 3-4 x (2 x 50 m) at ~90%; 6 x 45 m max; 3 x 300 m; 2 x 250 m; 5 x 200 m; 350/250/150 ladder. | Troy Johnson: <80 m ATP-CP sprints; 4-6 x 150 m; 2 x 3 x 200 m; 6-10 x 200 m; 4-6 x 300 m; 3 x 350 m; 3 x 300 m.
dose_raw: Anderson: 3-4 x (2 x 50 m) at ~90%; 6 x 45 m max; 3 x 300 m; 2 x 250 m; 5 x 200 m; 350/250/150 ladder.
Troy Johnson: <80 m ATP-CP sprints; 4-6 x 150 m; 2 x 3 x 200 m; 6-10 x 200 m; 4-6 x 300 m; 3 x 350 m; 3 x 300 m.
protocols.rest_ratio: Anderson: 1 min rep / 2 min set (alactic 50 m); 3-4 min (6 x 45 m max); 8 min (3 x 300 m); 6 min (2 x 250 m); 5 min (5 x 200 m); 10-12 min and 6-8 min (350/250/150). | Troy Johnson: 'Sprints <80m rest for 1 set/3-4min' (ATP-CP); 4-7 min (4-6 x 150 m speed endurance); 5 min / 10 min sets w/ recovery jog (2 x 3 x 200 m); 3 min (6-10 x 200 m); 7-10 min (4-6 x 300 m special endurance); 3-5 min (6-10 x 200 m special endurance); full recovery (3 x 350 m lactate capacity); 7 min (3 x 300 m lactate threshold).
protocols.app_rule: Gives the exact speed-endurance vs special-endurance rest signatures used by practising 400 m coaches (speed-endurance 150s at 4-7 min vs special-endurance 300s at 7-10 min), so the knowledge base can contrast coaching practice against what the physiology (A10/A11) predicts.
protocols.caveats: COACH PRACTICE - these are clinic/university documents, not peer-reviewed studies; no control groups and no effect sizes. | The two coaches do not agree on rest values for the same workout label (200 m reps at 3, 5 or 10 min), so any single 'correct' rest for a labelled workout does not exist in this source set.

protocols.title: Optimal pacing for 400 m and 800 m: world records are POSITIVE splits - Reardon 2013
protocols.protocol: Split analysis of IAAF-ratified world records (Table I), men: 100 m 0 positive / 6 negative; 200 m 0 positive / 6 negative; one-lap (400 m / 440 yd) 25 POSITIVE / 0 negative; two-lap (800 m / 880 yd) 27 positive / 2 negative; mile 19 positive / 12 negative; 3000 m 12/9; 10,000 m 22/16. Women: 200 m 0 positive / 3 negative; one-lap 9 positive / 0 negative; two-lap 12 positive / 1 negative. | Verbatim: 'All world records for the 100 m and 200 m have been set with negative splits... All world records for one-lap races have been set with positive splits (second half slower than first half), and almost all records for two-lap races have been set with positive splits.' | Model result: there exists a critical distance Dc = 291 m. Below Dc the optimal strategy is maximal propulsive force for the whole race (which is why 100 m and 200 m records are negative splits - inertia at the start dominates); above Dc the optimum is ~2 s at maximum force then near-constant speed. | Mathematically: for A(v) with exponent n>1 the optimal speed decreases monotonically (positive splits); negative splits require n<1. A physically reasonable A(v) with dA/dv>0 and d2A/dv2>0 therefore implies optimal pacing REQUIRES positive splits. | Tested against the men's 400 m world record (Michael Johnson, 43.18 s): the X-factor (entropy accumulation) model matched every split time more closely than either the energy-depletion (ED) or maximal-anaerobic-power (MAP) models (ED model raced to 43.27 s, MAP to 44.31 s, before rescaling). | Observed characteristic: a velocity decrement of approximately 20% below maximum velocity during the latter three-fourths of the race is typical of 400 m world-class, national-class and regional-class athletes. | The paper's practical conclusion, verbatim: runners in 400 m and 800 m 'are often urged to attempt to run the second half of the race at the same pace as the first (even splits)... However, almost no successful runners in 400- and 800-m races actually do this.' | Weight-training interpretation: sustained contraction at >60-70% of maximum voluntary force can occlude muscle blood flow; the paper speculates that the slow, heavy squats favoured by sprinters aid 400 m/800 m performance by improving the working muscles' ability to clear accumulated 'X-factor' (best thought of as entropy) by diffusion. Suggested shape: ~70% of max load, moving slowly, ~10 s per up-and-down repetition.
protocols.dose: Weight-training shape as speculated in the paper: ~70% of the maximum load for the exercise, ~10 s per complete up-and-down movement (deliberately slow-tempo squats); no set/rep count is given - 'not specified in source'. | No running training dose is specified anywhere in the paper - it is a pacing/model paper.
dose_raw: Weight-training shape as speculated in the paper: ~70% of the maximum load for the exercise, ~10 s per complete up-and-down movement (deliberately slow-tempo squats); no set/rep count is given - 'not specified in source'.
No running training dose is specified anywhere in the paper - it is a pacing/model paper.
protocols.rest_ratio: not specified in source (pacing paper; no training rest intervals given)
protocols.app_rule: The clearest evidence that successful 400 m running is NOT evenly split: 25 of 25 men's one-lap world records and 9 of 9 women's were positive splits, with ~20% velocity decrement over the last three-quarters, while all 200 m records were negative splits.
protocols.caveats: This is a physics teaching paper (Am J Phys), not exercise physiology - the 'X-factor' is explicitly left unspecified and is 'best thought of as entropy', so the biochemical identification of fatigue is the author's speculation. | The world-record split data is a selected sample (only records with published halfway splits, as ratified by the IAAF). | Dc = 291 m is a model output dependent on the assumed metabolic parameters.

protocols.title: Modifying 200 m pacing strategy: moderate the first 100 m, maximise the second - 20.43 s to 20.14 s
protocols.protocol: Three-part design: (1) cross-sectional analysis of 53 official 200 m races by world-class sprinters; (2) longitudinal analysis of 8 official races by one elite Japanese sprinter (MS, 100 m PR 10.14 s, 200 m PR 20.43 s); (3) an intervention applying a modified pacing strategy. | Indices used: %ST = each 10 m split time as a percentage of the 200 m record; %PR = each 100 m split time as a percentage of the 100 m personal record. | Cross-sectional result: world-class sprinters 'tended to sprint relatively slow in the first half and faster in the second half of the 200 m' - the better 200 m runs are effectively negative-split in shape, matching Reardon's finding for the 200 m (A13). | Longitudinal result: MS ran faster overall times when his 100-200 m segment speed was higher. | Correlations with the 200 m race record (Table 1): running speed 100-200 m r = -0.965 (significant) vs 0-100 m r = -0.302 (ns). %ST 0-100 m r = -0.866 and %ST 100-200 m r = +0.866 (both significant). Step frequency 100-200 m r = -0.646; step length 0-100 m r = 0.402. | THE INTERVENTION PROTOCOL (exact): MS performed sprint sessions focused on pacing TWICE WEEKLY from 1 July to 17 August 2024 at distances of 120, 150, 200 and 250 m. In each drill he had to complete the FIRST 100 m in no less than 10.60 s, regardless of total distance, then sprint maximally over the final 100 m. For 200 m repetitions he was additionally instructed to control speed to the 80 m mark, re-accelerate between 80 m and 110 m (curve exit), and sprint the last 100 m at maximal effort. Other training loads were kept consistent with previous levels. | Outcome: the 200 m record improved from 20.43 s to 20.14 s (0.29 s / ~1.4%) in an official national race. | Supporting mechanism: in 400 m races a driven pacing strategy at around 93% of the 200 m personal best has been linked to smaller declines in both step frequency and step length in the second half - the paper transfers this logic to the 200 m. | Rationale for the 200 m specifically: the event demands high step FREQUENCY (not primarily stride length) in the latter half, facilitated by short ground contact times; anaerobically, 200 m performance appears to depend on anaerobic work capacity, with ATP-PCr and muscle glycogen falling rapidly at the onset of the sprint.
protocols.dose: Intervention: 2 sprint sessions per week, 1 July - 17 August 2024, at 120 m, 150 m, 200 m and 250 m. | Per-rep pacing constraint: first 100 m no faster than 10.60 s; final 100 m maximal. For 200 m reps: controlled speed to 80 m, re-acceleration 80-110 m, maximal final 100 m. | Daily training context: the athlete trained at least 3 h/day, 5 days/week (rep counts and set numbers are NOT given - 'not specified in source').
dose_raw: Intervention: 2 sprint sessions per week, 1 July - 17 August 2024, at 120 m, 150 m, 200 m and 250 m.
Per-rep pacing constraint: first 100 m no faster than 10.60 s; final 100 m maximal. For 200 m reps: controlled speed to 80 m, re-acceleration 80-110 m, maximal final 100 m.
Daily training context: the athlete trained at least 3 h/day, 5 days/week (rep counts and set numbers are NOT given - 'not specified in source').
protocols.rest_ratio: not specified in source (recovery between reps and between sets is not reported)
protocols.app_rule: The only fetched source giving an actual 200 m pacing-intervention protocol with a constraint time (first 100 m >= 10.60 s) and a measured race outcome (20.43 -> 20.14 s), plus correlation evidence (100-200 m speed r = -0.965) that the second 100 m governs 200 m performance.
protocols.caveats: Exp. 3 is a single-athlete case study - no control and no replication; the 0.29 s gain cannot be attributed to pacing alone (the athlete continued full training). | Cross-sectional correlations come from broadcast-derived splits (29.97 fps video analysis in the intervention; the %PR analysis used 46 races because 7 sprinters lacked a same-season 100 m record). | The paper reports no rest intervals or rep counts, so the protocol cannot be reproduced in full from this source.

protocols.title: Clyde Hart's 400 m programme: 200 m-split race model, workout categories and actual weekly doses (Baylor)
protocols.protocol: RACE MODEL / 200 m SPLIT RELATIONSHIP (verbatim): 'the outstanding 400 meter runner will have approximately a one second deferential between their best open 200 meters and the time it takes them to run the first 200 meters of the 400 meter dash. The less experienced 400 meter runner should have approximately a two-second deferential.' | 400 m time prediction formula from a 200 m time: 'double the time of their best open 200 meters then add 3.5 seconds to this.' | Energy framing: 'The 400 meters is an oxygen-deficient event... The energy used during the 400 meter run is derived from the breakdown of high energy phosphate compounds and from the splitting of glycogen to lactic acid. This event will rely primarily on two anaerobic systems--the ATP-PC and lactic acid systems.' The Baylor slides contrast 'Past approach: 90% anaerobic and 10% aerobic' with 'New approach: aerobic training can be as much as 40%'. | RACE SEGMENTATION (Baylor slides): 'Runner should think of the race as 4 different races -- First 100 meters pushed hard. Second 100 meters paced to within 1 second of best 200 time. Third 100 is positioning so as to be even or even ahead out of the turn. Fourth 100 is focused on keeping good technique and trying not to decelerate or tighten up at the finish.' Ideal race pattern = 'smooth deceleration' with as little tightening at the finish as possible. | SPEED ENDURANCE definition and dose rule (verbatim): 'This is running where the runner incurs a high oxygen debt, and there is a definite lactic acid buildup... Distances that are run can vary from 100 to 600 meters. Number of repetitions is figured by multiplying the race distance 2 1/2 times; in this case this would be about 1000 meters. The recovery period will usually be around 10 minutes - this is to give the runner almost full recovery so that there will be quality in the runs.' | Hart's speed-endurance workout menu: (a) 10 x 100 m, 5-10 min rest; (b) 6 x 150 m, 5-10 min rest; (c) 5 x 200 m, 10 min rest; (d) 4 x 300 m, 10 min rest; (e) 3 x 350 m, 10 min rest; (f) 2 x 450 m, 10 min rest. | TEMPO ENDURANCE (aerobic, 'quantity not quality'): rest generally 2-3 min. Examples: 8 x 200 m, 2 min rest; 6 x 300 m, 2 min rest; 50-100-150-200-300-350 with walk-same-distance recovery. | STRENGTH ENDURANCE (activities longer than 10 s): 6 x 150 m hill; 6 x 60 stadium steps; 6 x 15-second long-rope runs. | ENDURANCE RUNNING: pure aerobic continuous runs of 15-45 min. SPEED: full-speed runs of 30-150 m with long rest. POWER SPEED: fewer than 10 s duration, emphasising speed of muscle contraction. | Training year divided into four segments: off-season (Sept-Dec), early competitive (Jan-Feb), mid-season (Mar-Apr), late season (May-Jun). | SAMPLE WEEK (exact doses from the fetched Hart document): Monday - 2 x 600 m at 60 s pace with 15 min rest, then 3 x 300 m at 50 s with 1 min rest, then 3 x 300 m at 40 s with 5 min rest; Tuesday - 10 x 200 m at 30 s with 3 min rest plus 6 x 150 m long-hill; Wednesday - 4 x 350 m event runs at 48 s with 10 min rest (first 50 m fast, next 50 relaxed, 200 m split 28 s, then 100 m picked up, last 50 steady) plus 3 x 200 m at 30-29-28 s with 3 min rest; Thursday - 600-400-200-400-600 at 30 s pace with 5 min rest. | Programme philosophy (Baylor slides): 'Better to be under-trained than over-trained'; 'Rest should be as short as possible'; 'Stress and lactic acid build up comes only after a moderate run of around 40 seconds'; 'Continually reloading will keep 400 runner strong, fresh and able to continue to get better'; 'Treat the season as if it were several mini seasons'; goal = 'run fast at start of season and faster at the end'.
protocols.dose: Speed endurance: 10 x 100 m / 6 x 150 m / 5 x 200 m / 4 x 300 m / 3 x 350 m / 2 x 450 m; total session volume ~2.5 x race distance (~1000 m). | Tempo endurance: 8 x 200 m or 6 x 300 m; ladder 50-100-150-200-300-350. | Strength endurance: 6 x 150 m hill / 6 x 60 stadium steps / 6 x 15-s rope runs. | Sample week: Mon 2 x 600 m (60 s) + 3 x 300 m (50 s) + 3 x 300 m (40 s); Tue 10 x 200 m (30 s) + 6 x 150 m hill; Wed 4 x 350 m (48 s) + 3 x 200 m (30-29-28 s); Thu 600-400-200-400-600 (30 s pace).
dose_raw: Speed endurance: 10 x 100 m / 6 x 150 m / 5 x 200 m / 4 x 300 m / 3 x 350 m / 2 x 450 m; total session volume ~2.5 x race distance (~1000 m).
Tempo endurance: 8 x 200 m or 6 x 300 m; ladder 50-100-150-200-300-350.
Strength endurance: 6 x 150 m hill / 6 x 60 stadium steps / 6 x 15-s rope runs.
protocols.rest_ratio: Speed endurance: ~10 min between reps for the 200-450 m distances ('almost full recovery... so that there will be quality in the runs'); 5-10 min for the 100-150 m reps. | Tempo endurance: 2-3 min between reps (deliberately short; quality is not the aim). | Sample week: 15 min (2 x 600 m), 1 min (3 x 300 m at 50 s), 5 min (3 x 300 m at 40 s), 3 min (10 x 200 m and 3 x 200 m), 10 min (4 x 350 m event runs), walk-same-distance (ladder). | Hart's stated rationale for the ~10 min speed-endurance rest: to give 'almost full recovery' so the runs are high quality - explicitly the opposite intent of his 2-3 min tempo rest.
protocols.app_rule: The priority coach-practice source for this lane: it supplies the 200 m-split rule (1 s differential for the elite, 2 s for the developing runner), a 400 m prediction formula (2 x 200 m + 3.5 s), the four-segment race model, and a complete numeric speed-endurance/tempo menu with rest intervals, including the 3 x 350 m and 4 x 300 m shapes.
protocols.caveats: COACH PRACTICE, not peer-reviewed research - no control group and no effect sizes; the 'New approach: aerobic training can be as much as 40%' slide is assertion, not data. | The two Hart PDFs overlap but are not identical; some sample-week detail appears in only one of them. | The 1 s / 2 s 200 m differential is a rule of thumb from one coach's programme, not a population statistic.

protocols.title: Tapering for speed-power/sprint events: the numeric prescriptions (volume cut, duration, intensity maintenance)
protocols.protocol: Bosquet 2007 meta-analysis (27 of 182 screened studies met inclusion; pooled swimmers/runners/cyclists/triathletes): optimal taper = 2-week duration (overall effect 0.59+/-0.33, P<0.001) with training volume DECREASED EXPONENTIALLY BY 41-60% (overall effect 0.72+/-0.36, P<0.001), WITHOUT any modification of training intensity (effect 0.33+/-0.14, P<0.001) or frequency (effect 0.35+/-0.17, P<0.001). | Bosquet 2007 on the range of prior practice: 'Some studies have suggested that the reduction in training volume should be substantial, somewhere near 85% of normal training volume, whereas others have reported similar improvements in performance after a 31% reduction', and the volume decrease 'is generally obtained through the decrease in the duration of each training session'. | Tapering review: overall effect size for performance change when training intensity was REDUCED was -0.02 (95% CI -0.37 to 0.33), versus 0.33 (0.19-0.47) when intensity was MAINTAINED or increased. Maximal gains occur at a 41-60% volume reduction. | Tapering review on duration: 'A taper duration of 8 to 14 days seems to represent the borderline between the positive influence of fatigue disappearance and the negative influence of detraining.' | Tapering review on pre-taper load: a 20% increase over normal training for 28 days before the taper requires a step load reduction of approximately 65% over three weeks (instead of two weeks with no overload). Thomas et al.: a taper may be optimised by INCREASING training load 20-30% during the final 3 days of the taper. | European elite sprint coaches survey (31 coaches, 100-400 m): traditional periodization used by 45%; a 10- to 15-day tapering phase used by 48%, comprising 'a reduction in volume, maintenance of intensity, and focus on correct technical execution'. | Mujika & Padilla's own dissemination of the taper evidence: maintain training intensity; reduce volume by 41-60%; maintain frequency at >80%; individualise taper duration between 4 and 28 days; use progressive, nonlinear designs; expect performance improvements of ~3% (range 0.5-6.0%). | Team-sports taper meta-analysis (PubMed 32172680): taper duration ranges from 7 to 21 days with an average of 14 days; volume reductions from about 20% to about 60%; suppressing 2-3 sessions/week equals a 20-40% volume reduction; a 17% reduction in training intensity was also reported to improve muscular performance in one study; a 20% training-load increase just before the taper can improve taper outcome (Thomas, Mujika & Busso 2008).
protocols.dose: Taper prescription (meta-analytic optimum): duration 2 weeks (8-14 days in the review); volume -41% to -60% (exponential/step/linear reduction); intensity UNCHANGED; frequency unchanged (maintain >80%); reduce volume by shortening session duration rather than dropping sessions. | With a preceding overload block: +20% load for 28 days beforehand requires an approximately -65% step reduction over 3 weeks. | Optional final-3-day load increase: +20-30%.
dose_raw: Taper prescription (meta-analytic optimum): duration 2 weeks (8-14 days in the review); volume -41% to -60% (exponential/step/linear reduction); intensity UNCHANGED; frequency unchanged (maintain >80%); reduce volume by shortening session duration rather than dropping sessions.
With a preceding overload block: +20% load for 28 days beforehand requires an approximately -65% step reduction over 3 weeks.
Optional final-3-day load increase: +20-30%.
protocols.rest_ratio: not specified in source (taper literature prescribes volume/intensity/frequency, not inter-rep rest)
protocols.app_rule: Supplies the actual numeric taper envelope for speed-power events: 8-14 days (2 weeks optimal), cut volume 41-60%, change nothing else - and the elite-sprint-coach consensus of a 10-15 day taper with volume down and intensity maintained lines up with it.
protocols.caveats: CRITICAL GAP: there is NO meta-analysis or RCT of tapering in 200 m/400 m track sprinters. Bosquet's pooled effect covers swimmers, runners, cyclists and triathletes; the 41-60% / 2-week figures are a cross-sport optimum, not sprint-specific. | The 10-15 day figure (48% of surveyed European sprint coaches) is self-reported practice, not a measured optimum; the IJSPP source was abstract-level only (full text paywalled). | The Bosquet and tapering-review numbers originate largely from the same research group (Mujika), so they are not independent confirmations.

protocols.title: Sprint taper as actually run: final hard session 10 days out, step vs linear reductions (incl. a full Ben Johnson taper)
protocols.protocol: Sprint-specific taper duration guidance (verbatim): 'if prior training load is high, up to three weeks may be required [to taper]; if prior training load is low, then 3-5 days may be sufficient.' | 'The final hard session is ten days before the race, followed by a large reduction in overall volume, but a maintenance of intensity.' | Step taper definition: 'in a 10-day step-wise taper, I might reduce my training load to 40% on day one, and maintain it there for the whole ten days.' Linear taper example: 'reducing training load in a linear fashion, perhaps by 10% per day.' | A complete day-by-day Ben Johnson taper before the 1987 Canadian Championships is reproduced: Day -10: 4 x 30 m blocks plus 80/100/120/150 m at high intensity; Day -9: 10 x 200 m tempo; Day -8: 4 x 30 m blocks plus 1 x 120 m submaximal; Day -7: 2 x 10 x 100 m tempo; Day -6: 4 x 30 m blocks plus 1 x 80 m submaximal; Day -5: rest; Day -4: 10 x 100 m tempo; Day -3: 4 x 30 m blocks; Day -2: rest; Day -1: pre-race activation; Day 0: race (result 9.98 s).
protocols.dose: Duration: up to 3 weeks (high prior load) or 3-5 days (low prior load); final hard session 10 days before the race. | 10-day step taper: hold load at 40% of normal for the entire 10 days. Linear alternative: reduce by ~10% per day. | Ben Johnson 1987 example above, with exact rep schemes: 4 x 30 m blocks repeatedly, 10 x 200 m tempo, 2 x 10 x 100 m tempo, 10 x 100 m tempo, and single submaximal 80-150 m runs.
dose_raw: Duration: up to 3 weeks (high prior load) or 3-5 days (low prior load); final hard session 10 days before the race.

Maximal velocity 10-30 m flying at >98%, rest 4-15 min, volume 50-150 m, next HIS 48-72 h. Sprint-specific endurance 80-150 m at >95%, rest 8-30 min, volume 300-900 m, next HIS 48-72 h. Speed endurance 60-80 m at 90-95%, rest 2-4 min (extended 8-15 min), volume 600-2000 m. Resisted sprints 10-30 m at 80-95% (loaded effort maximal), rest 3-6 min, volume 50-200 m. Assisted 10-30 m at <=105%, rest 5-15 min, volume <=100 m. Tempo 100-300 m at 60-70%, rest 1-3 min, volume 1000-2000 m, next HIS 24 h, run on grass. | Haugen 2019 weekly template across mesocycles: Mon sprint (hill -> resisted -> acceleration -> acceleration+Vmax), Tue strength, Wed tempo, Thu quality (speed endurance -> speed endurance -> Vmax -> sprint-specific endurance), Fri strength, Sat tempo, Sun off. | Haugen 2019: leading practitioners use 2:1 or 3:1 loading blocks (2-3 high-load weeks then 1 easy week). Elite recovery example: 4-6 x 150 m sprint-specific endurance with 20-30 min recovery; junior alternative 2-3 x 100 m with 10 min; rule of thumb 1-2 min recovery per second of sprinting. | Dan Pfaff's 3-day micro-cycle as described by Haugen: 'short accelerations on Monday, maximal velocity sprinting on Wednesday, and sprint-specific endurance on Friday.' | Hansen (coach practice, Charlie Francis's collaborator): Francis's original zones = high 95-100%, medium 75-95%, low below 75% of best performance; Hansen widened high to a 90-100% band and lowered low to <=70% (sometimes 65%). | Hansen on distribution: 'most of his top male sprinters had 35% of all of their training in the High intensity category, while the remaining Low intensity work comprised 65% of all training.' protocols.title: Long-to-short vs short-to-long periodisation: what the evidence actually supports for 200 m/400 m

This approach focuses on long distances in the early preparation period and progresses to short distances throughout the training year.' | Haugen 2019: 'An even more popular periodization model for sprinters was introduced by Charlie Francis in the 1980s, termed short to long... the initial meso-cycles focus on short sprints and power training, culminating with the indoor season where 60 m is the main event. Maximal velocity is prioritized after the indoor season, while sprint-specific endurance becomes more prioritized when approaching the outdoor season... it is easier to improve maximal velocity and then extend the duration that velocity can be maintained.' | Haugen 2019's own evidence grade for periodisation (Table 6, verbatim): 'Variation/periodization - Poor agreement. It 'likely induces similar improvements to a traditional model in shorter events such as the 100-m swimming event.' | Matched-volume SST vs LST RCT (U19 males, n=18, 2x/week for 6 weeks; only difference = sprint distance, SST all sprints 20 m vs LST 40 m, total session volume matched): NO significant between-group differences in 5/10/20/30/40 m sprint or agility (p>0.05). He ran long-to-short as an athlete at McGill and later adopted short-to-long ideas from Charlie Francis; he selects between them using injury history (frequent hamstring injury -> short stuff, e.g. 30 m) and the trajectory of the athlete's times. protocols.title: Top-speed determinants: ground force vs limb repositioning speed
protocols.protocol: Weyand and colleagues tested the hypothesis with two experiments (level running across a range of speeds in fast vs slow runners, and declined vs inclined running in the same runners, using a force-plate treadmill). At top speed, swing times of fast and slow runners converged to nearly the same minimum values, so minimising swing time did not explain the difference in top speed. The difference came from the average mass-specific vertical force applied during foot-ground contact, which increased step length (L_step = L_c * t_step/t_c; F_avg/W_b substituted for t_step/t_c). In the declined vs inclined comparison, force applied to the surface was the most important determinant of the higher declined top speed; contact lengths contributed only modestly and maximal stride frequencies contributed not at all. Contact time was defined as the time foot-ground force exceeded 0 N; swing time as stride time minus contact time.
protocols.dose: Not a training intervention - no sets, reps or loads. The study identifies the mechanical target (higher mass-specific vertical support force in a fixed or shorter contact window) rather than a prescription.
dose_raw: Not a training intervention - no sets, reps or loads. The study identifies the mechanical target (higher mass-specific vertical support force in a fixed or shorter contact window) rather than a prescription.
protocols.rest_ratio: Not reported (cross-sectional mechanics study; subjects ran maximal efforts at multiple speeds and inclinations).
protocols.app_rule: Sets the physical objective for max-velocity training: raise the average vertical support force applied in the contact window. Ground-contact time therefore becomes a key monitoring and exercise-selection variable, and strength/power work should be judged on force applied quickly rather than on limb speed in the air.
protocols.caveats: Mechanical inference from a force-plate treadmill study; does not test a chronic training intervention. 'Greater force' is a constraint, not a coaching cue - the force must still be applied in the correct direction and fraction of the gait cycle.

protocols.title: Best-practice session structure for elite sprint training (acceleration, max velocity, sprint-specific endurance, speed endurance)
protocols.protocol: Haugen et al. integrated scientific and best-practice literature for elite 100-m sprinting (position statement, Sports Med Open 2019). The 100 m is divided into acceleration, maximal velocity and deceleration (sprint-specific endurance); maximal velocity correlates highly with 100-m performance and the best sprinters accelerate over a longer distance. Step-averaged maximal horizontal power output in world-class sprinters was 30.3 +/- 2.5 W/kg (men) and 24.5 +/- 4.2 W/kg (women), typically reached after about 1 s of sprinting, with individual maxima of 36.1 and 29.3 W/kg. Strength and power training is performed 2-3 times per week in the preparation phase, sequenced as consecutive 4-6 week cycles through hypertrophy, maximal strength and then explosive strength/power/plyometrics; strength sessions are usually scheduled the day after sprint-specific work to avoid soreness when sprinting. Sprinting intensity is polarised (>=95% of maximal velocity to enhance performance, <70% to facilitate recovery), training is organised into 'heavy' and 'easy' weeks (leading practitioners use 2:1 or 3:1), and a 3-day microcycle is Mon short accelerations / Wed maximal velocity / Fri sprint-specific endurance. Two-thirds of hamstring injuries in competitive sprinters occurred in the transition period between specific preparation and competition season.
protocols.dose: Acceleration: 10-50 m, >98% max velocity, 2-7 min recovery between reps, session volume 100-300 m. Elite sprinters 40 m with 7-min recovery; young/untrained 20 m with 2-min recovery. | Maximal velocity: flying sprints with a rolling build-up (20-40 m run-in typical) followed by 10-30 m at maximum velocity, >98%, 4-15 min recovery between reps, session volume 50-150 m. | Sprint-specific endurance: 80-150 m (7-15 s efforts) at 95-100%, full recovery between reps and sets, session volume 300-900 m. | Speed endurance: 60-80 m reps at 90-95%, recovery 2-4 min between reps and 8-15 min between longer sets, session volume 600-2000 m. | Resisted sprints: 10-30 m, 80-95% of max velocity, 3-6 min recovery, session volume 50-200 m. | Assisted sprints: 10-30 m from a flying start, up to 105% of max velocity, 5-15 min recovery, session volume <=100 m. | Tempo runs: 100-300 m at 60-70% of maximal velocity with 1-3 min recoveries; ~2000 m per session in preparation, ~1000 m in competition.

Maximal velocity: flying sprints with a rolling build-up (20-40 m run-in typical) followed by 10-30 m at maximum velocity, >98%, 4-15 min recovery between reps, session volume 50-150 m.
Sprint-specific endurance: 80-150 m (7-15 s efforts) at 95-100%, full recovery between reps and sets, session volume 300-900 m.
Speed endurance: 60-80 m reps at 90-95%, recovery 2-4 min between reps and 8-15 min between longer sets, session volume 600-2000 m.
Resisted sprints: 10-30 m, 80-95% of max velocity, 3-6 min recovery, session volume 50-200 m.
Assisted sprints: 10-30 m from a flying start, up to 105% of max velocity, 5-15 min recovery, session volume <=100 m.
Tempo runs: 100-300 m at 60-70% of maximal velocity with 1-3 min recoveries; ~2000 m per session in preparation, ~1000 m in competition.
protocols.rest_ratio: Work-to-rest stated per row (e.g. speed endurance ~2 min between reps and ~8 min between series). Rule of thumb: 1-2 min recovery for every second of maximal sprinting. At least 48 h before the next high-intensity session for acceleration and resisted/assisted work; 48-72 h for maximal velocity, sprint-specific endurance and speed endurance; 24 h after tempo.
protocols.app_rule: Use as the session-construction template for a 100/200/400 program: pick the quality, then hold distance, intensity, recovery and session volume inside these windows, and schedule heavy/easy weeks in a 2:1 or 3:1 pattern.
protocols.caveats: Best-practice ranges, not a controlled dose-response study. The review itself notes large gaps between science and best practice, publication bias toward positive findings, and that most experimental data come from untrained or moderately trained performers, so effect sizes in the literature overstate what elite sprinters can expect. | The review explicitly states the lowest effective sprinting intensity for stimulating adaptation is not established by research (most practitioners argue 92-95% of Vmax is required).

protocols.title: Resisted sprint training for acceleration: does it beat unresisted sprinting?
protocols.protocol: Systematic review and meta-analysis of resisted sprint (RS) training for acceleration. Pooled result: RS training did not yield greater improvements in sprint performance than unresisted (UR) training (ES = 0.1085, 95% CI -0.0129 to 0.2300, z = 1.7521, p = 0.0798) across the cumulative 15 studies published 2005-2022. Studies ranged from 8 to 24 sessions (14.7 +/- 5.3 sessions) over 4 to 10 weeks (7 +/- 1 weeks); intervention length 4-10 weeks (mean 7 +/- 2), session duration 30-90 min (mean 54.9 +/- 18.6 min). Resistance loads varied from an estimated 6.8% to 89.1% body mass (mean 34.3 +/- 28.9% BM). Bachero-Mena and Gonzalez-Badillo compared 5%, 12.5% and 20% BM: all three groups improved 0-40 m, but the heavy group also improved 0-20 m and 0-30 m, i.e. heavier loads favoured initial acceleration. Among recreationally active males training at 20%, 40%, 60% and 80% BM, velocity improvements occurred at 40% and 60% BM but not at 80% BM. In trained athletes (female rugby players, 80-90% BM; amateur male soccer players at 50% of max velocity using 80% BM loads), UR and RS groups both improved with only small UR gains vs moderate RS gains, and the two RS loads were not different from each other. Recent studies using 20% to >90% BM with a UR comparison group found no between-group differences.

protocols.app_rule: Resisted sprinting is a supplement to, not a replacement for, unresisted sprinting. Match the load to the athlete's training status: very heavy loads were unproductive in athletes without a sprint training background, while trained athletes tolerated 80-90% BM. Where the goal is initial acceleration, loads in the 20-60% BM band produced the clearest gains in lighter-trained groups.

protocols.title: Resisted vs assisted vs uphill-downhill sprint training: effects on kinematics, acceleration and maximum velocity
protocols.protocol: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the longitudinal (chronic) effects of resisted, assisted and uphill-downhill sprint training on sprint kinematics, acceleration and maximum velocity. No significant effects on changes in maximum velocity were found either in the analysis of all studies or in the resisted, assisted and uphill-downhill subgroups (Z = 0.06, p = 0.95; Z = 0.7, p = 0.48; Z = 0.09, p = 0.93; Z = 1.4, p = 0.16). The assisted sprint training group did not exhibit a significant improvement in maximum velocity. The combined group showed no significant change in maximum velocity, although a moderate within-group effect size was observed. Interventions were characterised by load expressed as velocity decrement and by session volume in metres, e.g. Cahill et al. 2 sessions/week, 90-420 m per session on a hard surface at 25%, 50% and 75% velocity decrement (radar measured); Kristensen et al. 3 sessions/week, 110 m per session, assisted 6% faster than normal sprinting and resisted at 6% velocity decrement; Sinclair et al. 2 sessions/week, 180 m per session at 20% maximum-velocity decrement; Spinks et al. 2 sessions/week, 215-340 m per session at 10% maximal velocity decrement.

protocols.title: Resisted sprint load selection: velocity-decrement bands and what each load develops
protocols.protocol: Coach-education best-practice synthesis of resisted sprint training for acceleration and maximum velocity. Velocity-decrement bands: light <10%, moderate 10-15%, heavy 15-30%, very heavy >30% slower than normal sprint (Alcaraz 2009; Haugen et al. 2019). Lighter resistances (~10% velocity loss) preserve form and are thought to target top-speed mechanics; heavier loads (30%+ velocity reduction) provide a bigger strength stimulus for acceleration. In youth footballers, both heavy (~75% velocity reduction) and light (~25% reduction) sled training improved sprint performance, with heavy loads giving slightly greater acceleration-phase gains and lighter loads more strongly improving maximum velocity (Baena-Raya 2025). Traditional guidance limited sled loads to <10% speed loss or 10% body mass; some sports scientists argue the optimal load for maximising power may be ~50% velocity reduction (Bolger 2015; Cross 2017). A review of 11 studies found no conclusive evidence that heavy sled training harms sprint times (Petrakos 2016). UK Athletics advocate light resistances only; some elite Jamaican sprinters used very heavy sled pulls up to 100% of bodyweight. Practical sliding scale: roughly 10-30% of body mass on a sled (or ~5-30% speed decrement).
protocols.dose: Distances: 5-20 m for acceleration with substantial resistance; 20-40 m with very light loads (~5-10% speed loss) or small parachutes when overloading the speed phase; uphill 10-30 m (commonly 20-30 m off-season). Resisted efforts kept under 50 m, typically 10-30 m. | Reps per set: 4-8 sprints per set for heavy resisted runs; up to 8-12 for lighter resisted runs. Examples: 5-6 x 10 m sled pulls (heavy) or 8 x 20 m sled runs (moderate). | Reported quality-limited rep counts at 80% of max sled load: ~5-8 reps before 0-20 m performance degraded, versus 10-12 quality reps at a 30% load. | Sets: 1-3 sets of high-quality reps, e.g. 2 sets of 5 x 15 m sled pulls. | Total volume: ~6 reps for a heavy session up to 15-20 total reps for lighter/mixed sessions; a youth study used 140-300 m total sprint distance per session (10-15 reps of 10-20 m) twice per week.

Reps per set: 4-8 sprints per set for heavy resisted runs; up to 8-12 for lighter resisted runs. Examples: 5-6 x 10 m sled pulls (heavy) or 8 x 20 m sled runs (moderate).

The source notes unresisted sprints are typically given 2-7 min per rep elsewhere in the sprint literature but does not state a per-rep rest for resisted work - treat the per-rep rest as implied rather than prescribed here.
protocols.app_rule: Match the load to the target: light (<10% Vdec) when the goal is mechanics and top-speed exposure, 10-30% BM bands for acceleration/horizontal force, very heavy only for athletes who can hold posture. Pair heavy resisted reps with unresisted sprints in the same session so the athlete immediately rehearses mechanics at speed.

protocols.title: Velocity-based resisted sprint prescription: individual load-velocity profiling and sled friction
protocols.protocol: Jean-Benoit Morin's practitioner article on sprint velocity-based training argues that resisted sprint prescription lags gym-based VBT. A sled-track coefficient measured on the testing day was 0.33 (24 kg total sled load produced a pulling resistive load of 8 kg; 8/24 = 0.33), so the same nominal sled load yields very different resistive loads, running velocities and neuromuscular overload across surfaces and conditions. The method: measure sprint velocity across a range of sled loads to build an individual load-velocity relationship, then prescribe the load that produces the intended velocity decrement (%Vdec) from the athlete's own maximal value. Cited primary sources: Cahill et al. Sled-Pull Load-Velocity Profiling and Implications for Sprint Training Prescription in Young Male Athletes (Sports 2019); Cross et al. Optimal Loading for Maximizing Power During Sled-Resisted Sprinting (IJSPP 2017); Cross et al. Determining friction and effective loading for sled sprinting (J Sports Sci 2017).
