protocols.title: Optimal sled load for maximising power, and resisted sprinting for maximum speed
protocols.protocol: Practitioner evidence review on whether resisted sprint training increases max speed. Cross et al. proposed an optimal load (Lopt) of 69-96% of body mass for heavy sled resisted sprinting, versus traditional loads proposed at <43% of body mass, and an optimal velocity decrement (Vopt) of 48-52% of the individual's maximal velocity versus traditional suggestions of <30% velocity decrement. Kawamori et al. compared 8 weeks of light loading (10% velocity decrease) with heavy loading (30% velocity decrease); the heavy group decreased sprint times significantly more than the light sled group, and the study concluded it had not determined an optimal load but that light resistance may be novel and that heavier resistance deserves more research. A single-participant pilot monitored with STATSports Sonra GPS showed max speed decreasing progressively as towed load increased across a sled intervention, and Dynamic Stress Load decreasing as the sled load got heavier despite the heavier loads being perceived as more tasking.
protocols.dose: Sled loads discussed: traditional <43% BM; proposed optimal for power 69-96% BM. Velocity decrements discussed: traditional <30% Vdec; proposed optimal Vdec 48-52% of maximal velocity. Comparative intervention: light = 10% velocity decrease vs heavy = 30% velocity decrease, over 8 weeks. | The GPS pilot is a single-participant (n = 1) case and reports no sets, reps or rest intervals.
dose_raw: Sled loads discussed: traditional <43% BM; proposed optimal for power 69-96% BM. Velocity decrements discussed: traditional <30% Vdec; proposed optimal Vdec 48-52% of maximal velocity. Comparative intervention: light = 10% velocity decrease vs heavy = 30% velocity decrease, over 8 weeks.
The GPS pilot is a single-participant (n = 1) case and reports no sets, reps or rest intervals.
protocols.rest_ratio: Not reported. No rep/set rest structure is given in this source.
protocols.app_rule: When the target is mechanical power development, loads in the 69-96% BM range (or ~50% Vdec) are the reference point; when the target is sprint times, the source's own caveat is that the evidence for heavier loads beating lighter/UR training is not settled.
protocols.caveats: The optimal-load proposal (69-96% BM; 48-52% Vdec) comes from power-maximisation analysis, not from a training-outcomes trial - heavy power-optimal loading may not translate into better sprint times. | The original study referenced by this article concluded it did NOT determine an optimal load. | The applied GPS evidence in this article is a pilot with n = 1 and cannot support a general dose recommendation.

protocols.title: Uphill sprinting as a resisted stimulus: gradient-to-velocity-loss relationship
protocols.protocol: Validation/reliability study in 24 collegiate athletes who sprinted maximally on flat terrain and on purpose-built turf hills of 5.2%, 8.8% and 17.6% gradient, measured by radar. Load-velocity relationships were valid (R2 = 0.99) and reliable (TE < 4.4%). The slope of the gradient-velocity relationship was -1.7 +/- 0.1%: every 1% increase in incline cost about 1.7% of maximal velocity. Athletes reached 92 +/- 2%, 87 +/- 2% and 75 +/- 3% of their maximal flat-terrain velocity on the 5.2%, 8.7% and 17.6% hills. All hills represented low resistance relative to the full load-velocity spectrum (<25% velocity loss). Because the maximal mechanical power zone of the velocity-power curve sits at about 50% of maximal velocity, hills up to 17.6% do not provide sufficient resistance to optimise power development; they can however develop late-stage technical ability because of the prolonged horizontally oriented body position. Athletes with greater horizontal force output at high velocities on flat terrain were most affected by gradient.
protocols.dose: Testing protocol: ~30 min warm-up including submaximal ~30 m sprints up to ~90% of self-selected maximal velocity, 5 min passive rest, then two maximal sprints on each of three hill gradients (5.2, 8.7, 17.6%) and three sprints on flat terrain in randomised order - 9 sprints total, each 30 m maximal from a two-point split stance. | Velocity loss per condition: 5.2% gradient = 8% slower; 8.8% gradient = 13% slower; 17.6% gradient = 25% slower (equivalent to 92%, 87% and 75% of flat maximal velocity). | To reach the ~50% Vdec needed for power optimisation would require roughly a 35% gradient.
dose_raw: Testing protocol: ~30 min warm-up including submaximal ~30 m sprints up to ~90% of self-selected maximal velocity, 5 min passive rest, then two maximal sprints on each of three hill gradients (5.2, 8.7, 17.6%) and three sprints on flat terrain in randomised order - 9 sprints total, each 30 m maximal from a two-point split stance.
Velocity loss per condition: 5.2% gradient = 8% slower; 8.8% gradient = 13% slower; 17.6% gradient = 25% slower (equivalent to 92%, 87% and 75% of flat maximal velocity).
To reach the ~50% Vdec needed for power optimisation would require roughly a 35% gradient.
protocols.rest_ratio: 2-3 minutes of recovery between the testing sprints (9 sprints total). This is a testing rest interval, not a training prescription - the source does not give sets/reps for hill training sessions.
protocols.app_rule: Treat hills as a technical/late-acceleration constraint rather than a power-development tool: use gradients under ~10% where between-athlete variability is lower, and use sleds or motorised devices when >30-50% Vdec is the objective.
protocols.caveats: The paper reports testing rest intervals only; no hill-training sets x reps x rest prescription is given. | Gradient effects are individual: steep hills (>15%) impact athletes differently, and athletes with higher horizontal force at speed were most affected. | The study tested acute velocity loss, not chronic hill-training adaptations.

protocols.title: Plyometric training dose for sprint performance: volume, duration and session count
protocols.protocol: Meta-analysis of chronic plyometric training (PT) and sprint performance: 26 studies, 56 effect sizes. Strategies that maximised the probability of significantly greater sprint improvement were training volume for less than 10 weeks, a minimum of 15 sessions, and high-intensity programs with more than 80 combined jumps per session. Combining different types of plyometrics and using programs incorporating greater horizontal acceleration (sprint-specific plyometric exercises, jumps with horizontal displacement) was recommended over using only one form of jump training (p < 0.05). No extra benefits were found from doing plyometrics with added weight.
protocols.dose: Duration: <10 weeks. | Minimum 15 sessions. | More than 80 combined jumps per session for high-intensity programs. | Exercise selection: combine plyometric types, prioritising sprint-specific/horizontal-displacement jumps over a single jump form. | Added weight: no additional benefit - bodyweight plyometrics are sufficient.

Minimum 15 sessions.

protocols.caveats: The abstract reports aggregate dose-response trends rather than per-study sprint effect sizes. | No rest intervals between reps or sets are reported in this source, so a within-session rest structure cannot be taken from it.

protocols.title: Plyometrics and lower-limb performance: pooled effect sizes for sprint distances, jumps and reactive strength
protocols.protocol: Meta-analysis of plyometric training on lower-limb strength, power, agility and body composition in athletically trained adults: 70 studies, 1703 participants. Sprint: 10 m SMD = -0.50 (95% CI -0.86 to -0.14, p < 0.05); 20 m SMD = -0.53 (95% CI -0.90 to -0.17, p < 0.05); 30 m SMD = -0.57 (95% CI -0.93 to -0.20, p < 0.05); 5 m SMD = -0.29 (95% CI -0.58 to 0.00, p = 0.05) and 15 m SMD = -0.46 (95% CI -1.16 to 0.24, p = 0.20) were not significant. 1RM squat SMD = 0.53 (95% CI 0.23-0.84). Countermovement jump SMD = 0.69; squat jump SMD = 0.47; CMJ with arm swing SMD = 0.83; reactive strength index SMD = 0.80; standing long jump SMD = 1.34; Illinois test SMD = -0.64; T-test SMD = -0.41; body fat percentage SMD = -0.71. Heterogeneity was moderate for 10 m (I2 = 64%), 20 m (I2 = 62%) and 30 m (I2 = 63%). No significant gains for 5 m and 15 m sprints, VO2max, isokinetic strength at 60 deg/s, or lower-body jump power.
protocols.dose: Distance-specific pooled effects: 10 m SMD -0.50; 20 m SMD -0.53; 30 m SMD -0.57; 5 m SMD -0.29 (p = 0.05, not significant); 15 m SMD -0.46 (not significant). | Session-level sets, reps, contacts and rest are not reported at this level of the source.
dose_raw: Distance-specific pooled effects: 10 m SMD -0.50; 20 m SMD -0.53; 30 m SMD -0.57; 5 m SMD -0.29 (p = 0.05, not significant); 15 m SMD -0.46 (not significant).
Session-level sets, reps, contacts and rest are not reported at this level of the source.
protocols.rest_ratio: Not reported. Pooled meta-analytic effects; no per-session rest structure is given.
protocols.app_rule: Expect the largest transfer over 10-30 m; do not expect plyometrics alone to fix 5 m block clearance or 15 m. Pair plyometrics with strength work (1RM squat SMD 0.53) rather than substituting for it.
protocols.caveats: Sprint effects are small-to-moderate and heterogeneous (I2 ~62-64% at 10-30 m), so individual responses will vary widely. | 5 m and 15 m sprint effects were not significant, and lower-body jump power and isokinetic strength at 60 deg/s did not improve.

protocols.title: Plyometric frequency and session construction: contacts per session and rest between reps
protocols.protocol: Coach-education review of four key plyometric studies. (1) Low and moderate plyometric training frequency (1, 2 or 4 days per week over seven weeks) produced equivalent 20 m sprint improvements, so the 1 day/week program was the most efficient. (2) A 7-week program with only 15 minutes of plyometric work inside a half-hour session once weekly produced significant 20 m sprint improvement. (3) Rimmer & Sleivert (2000, JSCR) found plyometric training improved 40 m sprint times and was equally effective as sprint training; the improvement was explained by reduced ground contact time rather than by stride length or stride frequency, and was mainly in the acceleration phase (0-10 m) - bounding shares similar (longer) ground contact times with early acceleration. The sprint training group improved only in the 20-30 m interval, supporting combining plyometrics with sprint training. (4) A three-day-per-week plyometric program with high, intermediate and low intensity days totalled about 220 foot contacts (high day), 150-170 (intermediate day) and 120 (low day) in the sessions sampled.
protocols.dose: Frequency: 1-4 sessions/week all produced equivalent 20 m sprint gains over 7 weeks; 1 day/week was the most efficient. | Minimum effective session: ~15 minutes of plyometric work within a 30-minute session, once weekly, over 7 weeks. | Foot contacts in a structured 3-day/week program: high-intensity day ~220 contacts; intermediate day 150-170 contacts; low-intensity day ~120 contacts. | Set structure example from the sampled program: Session 1 (high intensity) 2 x 6, 1 x 4, 1 x 2; Session 2 (intermediate) 2 x 10, 2 x 8. | Sprint-specific plyometric session: bounding-type work, rest between reps 3-5 minutes to allow high recovery.

Minimum effective session: ~15 minutes of plyometric work within a 30-minute session, once weekly, over 7 weeks.
Foot contacts in a structured 3-day/week program: high-intensity day ~220 contacts; intermediate day 150-170 contacts; low-intensity day ~120 contacts.
Set structure example from the sampled program: Session 1 (high intensity) 2 x 6, 1 x 4, 1 x 2; Session 2 (intermediate) 2 x 10, 2 x 8.
Sprint-specific plyometric session: bounding-type work, rest between reps 3-5 minutes to allow high recovery.
protocols.rest_ratio: 3-5 minutes rest between plyometric repetitions to allow high recovery (stated for the sprint-specific plyometrics program). Between sessions, non-consecutive days in the 3-day/week example.
protocols.app_rule: For sprinters, one well-designed plyometric session per week over 7+ weeks is enough to move 20 m sprint time; use higher contact volumes (200+ per session) only on a genuinely high-intensity day and keep 3-5 min between reps so each is high quality.
protocols.caveats: Foot-contact counts and set structures come from one illustrative program, not from a pooled dose-response analysis. | Per-study contact volumes and rest intervals vary; only the sprint-specific program is documented here with a 3-5 min between-rep rest. | The 15-minute/1x-week result was a 20 m sprint outcome in a specific cohort and should not be extrapolated to top-speed development.

protocols.title: Post-activation potentiation: intensity, volume and rest for complex training
protocols.protocol: Systematic review of post-activation potentiation (PAP) in strength training (17 studies). PAP is used as the mechanism behind complex training - heavy resistance exercise performed prior to a biomechanically similar ballistic movement. Four variables act on the conditioning activity: intensity, volume (inversely proportional to intensity), resting time (conditioned by intensity and volume) and the biomechanical similarity of conditioning and subsequent activity. Findings: experienced athletes benefit more from a higher-volume potentiation bout (1-3 sets), especially when the optimal power load is used; intensities of 65% 1RM are valid with high volumes, but higher potentiation effects were achieved with 85-90% 1RM; higher intensities need longer rest intervals; around 7-8 minutes of rest should be allowed to dissipate fatigue, and self-selected rest intervals are also valid because they adjust quite precisely. Studies have used 3-5 sets at 60-100% 1RM with fixed rest intervals. Athletes with a higher proportion of type II fibres benefit more from heavy loads and longer rest intervals. Several included studies used athletes with a 1RM back squat of at least 2x bodyweight.
protocols.dose: Volume: 1-3 sets of the conditioning activity for experienced athletes (some included studies used 3-5 sets at 60-100% 1RM). | Intensity: 85-90% 1RM produces the greatest potentiation; 65% 1RM is valid only when paired with high volume. | Rest between the conditioning activity and the explosive effort: ~7-8 minutes (potentiation values have been reported to peak after 8 min or longer); self-selected rest is acceptable. | The higher the intensity, the longer the rest interval required.
dose_raw: Volume: 1-3 sets of the conditioning activity for experienced athletes (some included studies used 3-5 sets at 60-100% 1RM).
Intensity: 85-90% 1RM produces the greatest potentiation; 65% 1RM is valid only when paired with high volume.
Rest between the conditioning activity and the explosive effort: ~7-8 minutes (potentiation values have been reported to peak after 8 min or longer); self-selected rest is acceptable.
The higher the intensity, the longer the rest interval required.
protocols.rest_ratio: Rest interval 7-8 minutes between the heavy conditioning activity and the subsequent performance; longer for higher intensities. Note also that a set-to-set arrangement (complex training) implies a separate intra-complex rest that this paper addresses by intensity/volume.
protocols.app_rule: Before a sprint or jump session, use 1-3 sets at 85-90% 1RM of a biomechanically matched lift and then wait ~7-8 minutes before the explosive effort; do not shorten the rest after heavy singles.
protocols.caveats: PAP is a transient acute effect; the review notes less is known about whether acute potentiation translates into chronic adaptations. | The review notes that biomechanical similarity between the conditioning activity and the subsequent task is a crucial but under-controlled variable. | The effect depends on athlete training status and fibre type - untrained athletes and low-intensity protocols may see no benefit.

protocols.title: French contrast training: four-phase protocol and pooled sprint effect
protocols.protocol: Systematic review and meta-analysis of French contrast training (FCT) on lower-limb athletic performance in healthy adults. FCT significantly improved sprint performance (large effect: SMD = -0.92, 95% CI -1.30 to -0.55, p < 0.001) and jump performance (moderate effect: SMD = 0.62, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.91, p < 0.001). FCT consists of four sequential exercise phases: (1) heavy compound exercise (e.g. 80-90% 1RM squat); (2) plyometric exercise (e.g. vertical jump); (3) light-to-moderate load compound exercise that maximises movement velocity (e.g. ~30% 1RM barbell weighted jumps); (4) a plyometric exercise, often assisted. The rationale is to stimulate adaptations across the force-velocity curve in one session and to exploit post-activation performance enhancement. One included RCT (Meader et al. 2014) used: 1) back squat at 60-85% 1RM for 6-10 reps; 2) CMJ 6-10 reps; 3) loaded CMJ 6-10 reps; 4) band-assisted jump 6-10 reps, for 1-4 sets, 3 sessions/week for 12 weeks, and found sprint (50 m) improved. Kasim et al. recommended implementing complex training over 6-12 weeks at 2-3 sessions per week.
protocols.dose: FCT four-phase structure: (1) heavy compound 80-90% 1RM squat; (2) vertical/normal plyometric; (3) ~30% 1RM loaded jump; (4) assisted plyometric. | Example documented RCT: back squat 60-85% 1RM x 6-10 reps, CMJ x 6-10, loaded CMJ x 6-10, band-assisted jump x 6-10; 1-4 sets; 3 sessions/week; 12 weeks. | Recommended block length and frequency: 6-12 weeks at 2-3 sessions per week.
dose_raw: FCT four-phase structure: (1) heavy compound 80-90% 1RM squat; (2) vertical/normal plyometric; (3) ~30% 1RM loaded jump; (4) assisted plyometric.
Example documented RCT: back squat 60-85% 1RM x 6-10 reps, CMJ x 6-10, loaded CMJ x 6-10, band-assisted jump x 6-10; 1-4 sets; 3 sessions/week; 12 weeks.
Recommended block length and frequency: 6-12 weeks at 2-3 sessions per week.
protocols.rest_ratio: Not specified in the summary used here beyond the program-level frequency (2-3 sessions/week). Intra-set rest between the four FCT phases is not reported in this source - the PAP entry (B-12) covers the 4-8 min rest principle for heavy-to-explosive pairing but that interval is not stated here.
protocols.app_rule: Use FCT as a 6-12 week, 2-3 sessions/week block when the aim is simultaneous sprint and jump improvement; sequence one heavy lift into two plyometric movements and one assisted plyometric within the same complex.
protocols.caveats: FCT is the contrast variant with the strongest pooled sprint effect here, but the meta-analysis pools small trials with varied control conditions. | This source does not report the intra-complex rest intervals, so the rest structure must be taken from the PAP literature rather than assumed. | Jump effects were smaller (moderate) than sprint effects, which is an unusual pattern and warrants caution.

protocols.title: Relative squat strength and sprint times: 1RM/body mass benchmarks
protocols.protocol: Cross-sectional study of 17 Division I-AA male football athletes (height 1.78 +/- 0.04 m, body mass 85.9 +/- 8.8 kg, BMI 27.0 +/- 2.6 kg/m2, back squat 1RM 166.5 +/- 34.1 kg, 1RM/BM 1.94 +/- 0.33). Sprint times over 5, 10 and 40 yards were measured with infrared timing from a 3-point stance. Correlations with relative squat strength: 40 yd r = -0.6048 (power 0.7468, p = 0.0101); 10 yd r = -0.5437 (power 0.6255, p = 0.0241); 5 yd r = -0.4502 (power 0.4421, p = 0.0698, non-significant). Athletes were split at greater than 2.1 1RM/BM versus less than 1.9 1RM/BM: the stronger group had significantly lower 40 yd and 10 yd times (p <= 0.05), with no significant difference at 5 yards. Prior work: Wisloff et al. reported r = -0.940 between 10 m sprint time and squat 1RM; Harris et al. found non-significant correlations for machine squat 1RM (r = 0.200 and -0.140 for 10 m and 40 m); Kukolj et al. found no significant correlations for isometric knee/hip extensor or flexor peak force.
protocols.dose: 1RM back squat testing protocol: warm-up of multiple repetitions at 30% (8-10 reps), 50% (4-6 reps), 70% (2-4 reps) and 90% (1 rep) of estimated 1RM; squat depth to a 70-degree knee angle; up to 4 maximal attempts; 3-5 minutes rest between trials. | Relative-strength split used: >2.1 1RM/BM vs <1.9 1RM/BM (significant 10 yd and 40 yd advantage to the stronger group). | Cohort mean: 1RM/BM = 1.94 +/- 0.33.
dose_raw: 1RM back squat testing protocol: warm-up of multiple repetitions at 30% (8-10 reps), 50% (4-6 reps), 70% (2-4 reps) and 90% (1 rep) of estimated 1RM; squat depth to a 70-degree knee angle; up to 4 maximal attempts; 3-5 minutes rest between trials.
Relative-strength split used: >2.1 1RM/BM vs <1.9 1RM/BM (significant 10 yd and 40 yd advantage to the stronger group).
Cohort mean: 1RM/BM = 1.94 +/- 0.33.
protocols.rest_ratio: 3-5 minutes rest between 1RM attempts (testing protocol). Training set/rest structure is not part of this study.
protocols.app_rule: Use relative squat strength (1RM/BM) rather than absolute squat as the strength benchmark: below ~1.9x body weight is a reasonable flag for developing max strength; at or above ~2.1x the athlete is in the band associated with faster short sprints.
protocols.caveats: Correlational and cross-sectional - it does not show that raising squat strength causes faster sprinting. | The correlation at 5 yards was NOT significant, so maximal strength in this cohort related to 10-40 yd times more than to the very first steps. | Single-joint and machine strength measures show much weaker or null relationships (Harris et al.; Kukolj et al.), so the finding is specific to free-weight, multi-joint squat strength. | Small sample (n = 17) of male American football players - extrapolation to sprinters is an inference.

protocols.title: Olympic weightlifting derivatives: exercise menu, loading and set/rep prescription
protocols.protocol: Practitioner review of weightlifting derivatives for sports performance. Derivatives remove complexity from the competition lifts (no pull from the floor and/or no full catch) while preserving the triple-extension pattern common to sprinting, jumping and change of direction. Pulling derivatives (clean pull, snatch pull, hang high pull, jump shrug, mid-thigh pull) remove the catch and let the pull be overloaded: peak power in the clean pull and snatch pull occurs at 90-95% 1RM (1RM based on the full lift), with a corresponding drop in volume. Olympic lifts and derivatives avoid the deceleration phase inherent in traditional strength movements (which can have a deceleration period for up to 50% of the exercise), and many generate their highest power outputs at heavier weights (>70% 1RM) than traditional strength movements (>30% to <70% 1RM). Hori et al. 2008 found 1RM hang power clean significantly and positively correlated with maximal strength (p < 0.01), jumping (p < 0.05) and sprinting (p < 0.01). The NSCA position stand notes pulling derivatives can be prescribed at loads up to 120% of a 1RM catch variation from the floor and even 140% from the knee or midthigh, and that jump shrugs are programmed at 30-60% 1RM hang power clean.
protocols.dose: Power emphasis: 3-6 sets of 3-5 reps at 55-70% 1RM for derivative lifts (also confirmed as the intensity band where mid-thigh power clean, push press and squat jump peak power and rate of force production are maximised). | Heavier derivatives: ~70-90% 1RM for cleans and pulls to develop maximal strength and high-force production; lighter jump shrugs and hang power snatches at ~30-50% 1RM to emphasise velocity. | Clean pull / snatch pull: peak power at 90-95% 1RM (based on the full-lift 1RM); recommendations range from 3-5 sets of 1-3 reps at 85-100+% 1RM, with volume reduced as intensity rises. | Jump shrug: 30-60% 1RM hang power clean (NSCA position stand). | Highest power outputs occur at >70% 1RM for Olympic derivatives vs 30-70% 1RM for traditional strength movements.
dose_raw: Power emphasis: 3-6 sets of 3-5 reps at 55-70% 1RM for derivative lifts (also confirmed as the intensity band where mid-thigh power clean, push press and squat jump peak power and rate of force production are maximised).
Heavier derivatives: ~70-90% 1RM for cleans and pulls to develop maximal strength and high-force production; lighter jump shrugs and hang power snatches at ~30-50% 1RM to emphasise velocity.
Clean pull / snatch pull: peak power at 90-95% 1RM (based on the full-lift 1RM); recommendations range from 3-5 sets of 1-3 reps at 85-100+% 1RM, with volume reduced as intensity rises.
Jump shrug: 30-60% 1RM hang power clean (NSCA position stand).
Highest power outputs occur at >70% 1RM for Olympic derivatives vs 30-70% 1RM for traditional strength movements.
protocols.rest_ratio: Not reported in this source. Rest intervals between sets of derivatives are not stated - do not invent them.
protocols.app_rule: For power development use 3-6 x 3-5 at 55-70% 1RM; for strength-speed overload use pulls at 85-100+% 1RM with 3-5 sets of 1-3 reps and correspondingly lower volume; include derivatives where an athlete lacks the technical base for full lifts.
protocols.caveats: Correlational evidence (hang power clean and sprint speed) is not causal training evidence. | Pulling derivatives at 120-140% of a catch-variant 1RM are heavy overloads that require technical competence and coaching supervision. | Derivative vs full-lift equivalence for power development is reported in the literature but the source here is a practitioner review.

protocols.title: Ground-contact-time-based exercise selection for sprinters
protocols.protocol: Coach-education framework using measured ground contact times (GCT) to align exercise selection with the phase of the sprint being targeted. Sprint GCTs (measured by the author): step 0 (block clearance) 0.35-0.40 s; step 1 0.20 s; step 2 0.13 s; step 3 0.12 s; step 4 0.12 s; maximal velocity 0.08-0.10 s. Sled pulling changes this profile: with a 100 lb sled on turf, GCT fell to 0.15 s by step 5, whereas with a 200 lb sled GCT never went below 0.22 s by step 5 - so the heavier sled is more relatable to the first couple of steps and the lighter sled to mid-acceleration (5-15 m). Jump exercises are bucketed the same way: very early acceleration 0.31-0.40 s (36 in squat jump 0.40; 42 in reverse depth jump 0.35; 48 in walking CMJ 0.35; 36 in walking CMJ 0.33); early-to-mid acceleration 0.20-0.30 s (6 in single-leg horizontal depth jump 0.30; 24 in depth jump to 36 in box 0.28; 12 in single-leg depth jump 0.26; 18 in depth jump to 36 in box 0.25; single-leg cycle bound 0.22; 36 in reverse depth jump 0.20); mid-acceleration to maximal velocity 0.13-0.17 s (12 in depth jump to 12 in box 0.13-0.15; forward pogos 0.13-0.15; in-place pogos 0.13-0.17). Extensive tempo (6 x 150 m at 60-70% effort) produced GCTs of 0.11-0.13 s. Cited sled-load studies: 80% body mass sled loads were more effective than unresisted sprinting for improving 10 and 20 m acceleration in soccer players (Morin, Petrakos, Jimenez-Reyes, Brown, Samozino, Cross); loads producing a 30% increase in sprint times improved 5 m and 10 m acceleration, whereas loads causing a 10% increase gave only a smaller 10 m improvement and no 5 m improvement (Kawamori, Newton, Hori, Nosaka). Depth jump research (Washif & Kok): jump height, flight time and RSI of 35 cm depth jumps correlated significantly with faster sprint times; 50 cm depth jumps did not.
protocols.dose: Sled load selection by contact-time/position match: 200 lb sled for the first couple of steps; 100 lb sled for mid-acceleration 5-15 m (author's own turf data). | Jump exercise buckets by GCT: 0.31-0.40 s (very early acceleration), 0.20-0.30 s (early-mid acceleration), 0.13-0.17 s (mid-acceleration to maximal velocity). | Cited training-study loads: 80% BM sled (Morin et al.); sled loads causing 30% vs 10% increase in sprint times (Kawamori et al.). | Depth jump heights: 35 cm correlated with faster sprint times while 50 cm did not (Washif & Kok).

Jump exercise buckets by GCT: 0.31-0.40 s (very early acceleration), 0.20-0.30 s (early-mid acceleration), 0.13-0.17 s (mid-acceleration to maximal velocity).
Cited training-study loads: 80% BM sled (Morin et al.); sled loads causing 30% vs 10% increase in sprint times (Kawamori et al.).

protocols.title: Zone-matching: pairing the weight room with the sprint phase trained that day
protocols.protocol: Practitioner framework adapted from Stuart McMillan's zone-matching approach at ALTIS, used in a published full-year program for an elite female 200 m sprinter preparing for the 2019 World Championships. Ground contact times are roughly 0.15-0.20 s in acceleration and below 0.10 s at maximum velocity, which changes the force profile, joint torques and stretch-shortening-cycle demands. Zone 3 (max strength): acceleration - block starts, 0-30 m sprints, sled pushes, resisted accelerations; weight room - heavy back squat, trap bar deadlift, heavy split squat, slow eccentric loading. Zone 1 (speed-strength): max velocity - flying 20-30 m, wicket runs, sprint-float-sprint, top-speed holds; weight room - jump squat, power clean, fast Olympic pulls, reactive bounding, stiffness hops. Zone 2 (work capacity): speed/special endurance - 150-300 m reps, segment runs, intensive tempo, race-pace intervals; weight room - moderate load complexes (3-4 x 8), circuit-style supersets, hypertrophy work, general strength. Common errors: heavy squats after a max-velocity session (blurs the speed signal), and defaulting to light high-rep lifting on every gym day (misses the acceleration day opportunity). In competition phase, weight-room volume drops but the matching logic stays; a reduced-volume Zone 3 session (fewer sets, same intensity) still fits better after block work than switching to light circuits.

protocols.title: Flying 30 and sprint-float-sprint session construction
protocols.protocol: Coach-education article on constructing Flying 30 (and sprint-float-sprint) sessions. Set-up: an approach long enough for the sprinter to reach full speed (cone), then a 30 m speed zone (second cone). The sprinter must achieve maximum velocity BEFORE entering the zone or the drill becomes an acceleration drill. Approach distances: 20-25 m for slower/younger sprinters, roughly twice that for a good varsity sprinter, 30-35 m for some (e.g. varsity girls). The training bout consists of two sets of Flying 30s, each set corresponding to the five relaxation cues (shoulders, head, arms, hands, attitude), so the athlete focuses on one thing at a time. Between sets the athlete takes a 400 m walk; between the five reps within a set the athlete decelerates slowly out of the zone and takes a slow walk back. Stride-rate development options: downhill running over a 30 m zone on a 2-4% grade; Korchemni's stick drill with stick spacing reduced 5% (40:10 ratio, advanced 50:15) to force higher tempo; and a weighted vest where the load should not slow the sprinter by more than 8% through the zone. Stride-length development uses the stick drill on a downhill grade with spacing 5% greater than maximum stride length. Stop the workout whenever times drop off noticeably. The 30 m distance is a conditioning mode - use 20 m and 40 m zones as well. The 'six-second rule' underpins the relaxation cue: after six seconds in a 100 m race it is impossible to run faster, so the athlete must maintain rather than strain.

protocols.title: Acute effects of overspeed (towing) on sprint mechanics: what it actually changes
protocols.protocol: Systematic review with meta-analysis of the acute effects of overspeed stimuli using towing systems on athletic sprint performance: 16 studies, 240 men and 56 women. Acute responses: increase in maximum running speed (ES = 1.54, large), stride length (ES = 0.92, moderate), flight time (ES = 0.28, small) and stride rate (ES = 0.12, trivial); decrease in contact time (ES = 0.57, small). Analysis of reported ground reaction forces and electromyography data did not provide enough consistent evidence to conclusively determine whether the changes are due to a greater muscular response of the athlete or the effect of the towing system. Coach guidance from the same review: overspeed training should be used in a typical workout after a general warm-up including dynamic stretching, while athletes are fatigue free; because the purpose is to train the neuromuscular system rather than the anaerobic system, rest between repetitions must be sufficient to allow complete recovery.

protocols.title: Assisted and overspeed sprinting: loads, distances, session placement and recovery
protocols.protocol: Coach roundtable (1080 Motion Coaches Corner with Chris Korfist, Will Collins and Jake Cohen) on assisted and overspeed sprinting. Assisted sprinting helps athletes reach top speed faster and is used in-season, in sprint drills, or in return-to-play; overspeed sprinting pushes athletes beyond what they can do on their own, usually targeting speeds 5-10% faster than max velocity. Loads: most coaches stay between 3-7 kg, with lighter loads (~3 kg) for high-level sprinters to focus on clean mechanics and heavier loads (~6-7 kg) for bigger athletes or when targeting acceleration. Distances: 10-30 m for acceleration or heavier athletes; 60-90 m for track athletes or upright top-end speed. Timing: after a general prep or teaching phase (3-6 weeks), or as early as day 1 with proper cueing and assisted-sprint progressions, and in-season with lighter loads to maintain rhythm and speed exposure; also post-injury to reintroduce high-speed mechanics in a controlled way. Red flags before implementation: poor posture control, anterior pelvic tilt, inability to produce or maintain frontside mechanics. Coaches track top speed, the shape of the velocity-distance curve, 0-5 m splits and session-to-session trends. Korfist on recovery: 'This is a high neural demand. 12 to 20 minutes between reps isn't crazy if you're doing it right.'

protocols.title: Clyde Hart 400m training model: pace-percentage method, event-type diagnosis and annual emphasis structure
protocols.protocol: Hart's 400m model rests on distributing speed and energy as efficiently as possible over the whole race ('the 400 is not a full sprint'). Athletes are first classified as sprinter-types (200/400) or half-miler types (400/800); the aim is to diminish weaknesses and increase strengths. Anaerobic/lactic is the dominant system, but Hart's 'new approach' allows aerobic training to be as much as 40% of total volume (past approach was ~90% anaerobic / 10% aerobic). Overload follows a 'pyramid': repeated 2 x 600m through the 400m in a slowly-lowered pace; when the pace can no longer be held the distance drops to 500m at the SAME 400m pace, then again down to 450m, reached around mid-season and then continued to season's end; before a major competition a SINGLE run replaces the double. Lactic-acid rationale: a significant lactic build-up needs a hard run of about 40 seconds, hence the ideal repetition distance is ~300m for women and ~350m for men; several such reps fit in one session. Weekly skeleton is stable year-round (Mon quality 200s, Tue long reps, Wed 350s, Thu event/hill/speed, Fri similar/lighter) — Hart prized consistency, did not believe in peaking, refreshed the base rather than milking it, and preferred under-training to over-training.

protocols.title: Clyde Hart event runs and broken 400s — segment running at race pace with timed splits
protocols.protocol: Hart's 'Event Running' = running pre-determined race strategies over set distances, timed, to rehearse exactly how the 400m will be run ('segment running'). The race he is rehearsing: reach race speed within the first 50m, relax the upper body while maintaining leg speed, cruise through 200m (elite within ~1s of best open 200m), then a controlled pick-up — driving arms and lifting knees — from 200m to 300m so the athlete comes off the final curve even or ahead, then hold form while fighting fatigue over the last 100m. Reps are always timed and recorded, and athletes are told in advance the 200m and 300m checkpoints they must hit; Hart considered this pre-experienced pace the source of competitive confidence. The coach must be personally involved in race strategy, not just a trainer.

protocols.title: Clyde Hart speed work and 200m speed-endurance progression (the 400m-400/200m athlete)
protocols.protocol: Hart's speed work for long sprinters never exceeds 150m: 6 x 40m starts, 6 x 60m flying, 6 x 60m relay hand-offs, or a 30-40-50-60-70m progression on the bend with full recovery. His trademark '60-40m' session runs 60m at 95%, floats 40m, pitter-patter jogs 40m, then repeats — two laps per set, two sets, five minutes between sets — which rehearses maintaining cadence under rising fatigue without ever hitting 100%. For 200m speed endurance he used 6 x 100m at 95% from a standing start, non-timed, on 5 minutes rest. Crucially, Michael Johnson — a 19.32 200m runner — still did mostly 400m training; Hart's view is that speed is preserved by strength ('runners can't lose speed if they stay strong'), so the 200m quality is maintained through the 400m programme rather than a separate 200m plan. Speed at 100/200m is treated as an advantage only if the athlete learns to distribute it.

protocols.title: Long-to-short vs short-to-long for the 400m: definitions, argued trade-offs, and the four-week blended block templates
protocols.protocol: Long-to-Short: work backwards from the event — large volumes of relatively slow 300-600m reps and tempo build the aerobic/anaerobic base first and speed is protected and sharpened on top of it; the accepted cost is a slow athlete who is merely 'strong as a horse'. Short-to-Long: develop maximum speed first (acceleration 20-30m -> 50-60m -> 80-150m speed endurance) and add metabolic work only as far as it supports speed; the accepted cost is a thin aerobic/anaerobic base and a pre-competition phase short of race-specific endurance. Hiserman's argued position is that both philosophies contain necessary principles and that what is usually MISSING is a consistent, varying-volume presence of Maximum Speed and Maximum Strength/Power work in the Preparation and Pre/Early Season phases — he reports finding both a lack of maximum-speed work and an absence of race modelling using speed endurance / Special Endurance I in high-school plans. His operational answer is the rotating four-week block above, whose structure stays constant while session types advance: speed runs short-to-long (20m > 60m) and energy-system work runs long-to-short (600m > 300m reps), mixed with shorter extensive-tempo reps so the athlete adapts to higher speeds with shorter rest. Total sprint volume climbs across the block; energy-system volume climbs through the first half of Preparation then falls as intensity and rest rise. He also insists on identifying each athlete's fibre type and body type and weighting the plan toward that individual's weakness while keeping every component present.

protocols.title: Charlie Francis high-low system: intensity zones, CNS/ANS rationale and the 'never two high days back to back' rule
protocols.protocol: Francis's classification: every running session is either high (>=95% of best, full CNS activation, maximal recruitment, needs full recovery) or low (<75%, recuperative — improves blood circulation and capillary density and hastens recovery, with inherently low injury risk and safely accumulated volume). The 75-95% band he advocated avoiding, because it produces residual peripheral AND central fatigue and elevated soft-tissue injury risk without driving speed adaptation, and being non-circulatory it also impairs recovery. Consequence: the weekly microcycle is a 'high-low' alternation — 2-3 speed days separated by low-intensity days — so the CNS recharges and each high session can be performed at maximum output. In GPP, however, the week should be relatively FLAT (volume and variety emphasis, less day-to-day intensity contrast); going polarized too early causes an early plateau and the athlete never peaks in the competitive period. Age matters: young/beginner athletes operate at near-100% effort but do not generate the same true CNS fatigue, so their work is functionally high-intensity even at low absolute outputs; as training age rises, genuinely high outputs demand proportionally more low-intensity recovery. When conditions prevent high-intensity work (cold, snow), Francis replaced it with short starts, high-intensity drills, plyometrics, explosive throws and maximal explosive lifts — that aggregate should be at least one-third of all work in the inclement-weather phase.

protocols.title: Charlie Francis sample pre-competition microcycle for a well-conditioned sprinter: three speed sessions, three weights, one special-endurance session
protocols.protocol: Francis's template week for an advanced sprinter entering competition: Monday acceleration + block work + jumps/bounds + weights; Tuesday tempo; Wednesday max-velocity/top-speed work plus a short special-endurance block (2-3 x 200m) plus weights; Thursday the same tempo sets as Tuesday or 8 x 200m relaxed, flagged as a recovery day; Friday block starts, high-speed 60s and smooth 2 x 2 x 60m plus weights, cancelled if there is a Saturday competition; Saturday compete; Sunday rest. The parallel six-day rendering of the same system: Monday HIGH (short acceleration, max-strength lifting, explosive med-ball throws), Tuesday LOW (grass tempo sub-75%, circuits, core, therapy), Wednesday HIGH (flying sprints, long acceleration builds to max velocity, light plyometrics, strength-maintenance lifting), Thursday LOW (extensive tempo, grass strides, circuits, pool/bike, stretching), Friday HIGH (speed-endurance reps at 95-98% intensity, block starts, explosive lifting or med-ball work), Saturday LOW (very easy tempo, light circuits, active recovery), Sunday REST.

protocols.title: Boo Schexnayder: neural-day vs general-day session construction for speed-power athletes
protocols.protocol: Schexnayder assigns every session a theme. Ordering within the session is fixed and non-negotiable: a neural day starts, after warm-up, with acceleration and/or speed, then multi-jumps and plyometrics, then weight training. A general day starts with technique, then circuits or endurance work. This alternation is his answer to coaches worried about over-stimulating the CNS — it lets metabolic work be added without inhibiting speed or explosiveness, because the general days carry no major neural load. He also stresses that the event itself is the most important drill for any event: transfer from drills is low, and long approaches / full-approach jumps should be kept out of training in favour of 6-10 step runs so that more quality repetitions can be accumulated. Cross-country is counterproductive for sprinters and jumpers because the speeds are too low and endurance is addressed too much.

protocols.protocol: Pfaff builds sets from very short, maximum-quality accelerations: 5 x 3 x 10-40m with 3-5 minutes between runs is his canonical acceleration-development session, and he had sub-10 sprinters who never ran longer than 150m in training. Readiness is judged by postural integrity and fluidity: if postures change or the motion becomes mechanical, the session ends. Recovery is monitored with pulse rate, portable blood-lactate analysers and blood/urine chemistry. His explicit argument against the 400m-style diet of 10 x 200m intensive tempo and 500-400-300 sets is that sprint/jump athletes never encounter that sustained lactate environment in competition, so training there is misplaced; instead, lactate is produced on block/acceleration days and managed deliberately. Champion-ship demand is the exception he trains for: four races in two days produces steep lactate slopes, so athletes must learn to weather rapid lactate introduction and rapid clearance — which is not the same as sitting at a constant lactate level in tempo or interval work. He also maintains that 'more is better' is the single greatest myth in power-speed training.

protocols.title: The Speed Project 200m speed-endurance protocols and the two-week mid-season sprint block
protocols.protocol: The Speed Project's operating assumption is that speed endurance is a quality problem, not a volume problem: the same volume with 4 minutes between reps instead of 7-10 minutes produces visibly declining times across the reps, whereas the version with the longer rest keeps every rep at quality. Their four physiological barriers for the 200m are metabolic acidosis (hydrogen ion interference with the contractile mechanism), neuromuscular fatigue (ground contact times rise 15-20% in the final phase), mechanical breakdown (hip height drops, knee drive diminishes, contacts become passive) and fiber-specific exhaustion (fast-twitch fibres and phosphocreatine deplete first). Their methods: specific speed-endurance intervals with long rest, split runs to accumulate race-specific loading without technical collapse, speed-reserve development via progressive flying sprints to raise the speed ceiling (raising top speed from 10.5 to 11.0 m/s makes holding 95% far easier), and technique work under fatigue — e.g. 4-6 bounds focused on posture immediately after a hard 150m. Acid-buffering sets (2 x 4 x 200m, 30s between reps, 8 min between sets) are prescribed specifically to increase carnosine content and bicarbonate handling. Common mistakes they name: the volume trap, using tempo as a substitute for speed endurance, and scheduling high-intensity sessions too close together.

protocols.title: 200m race model (Pavlansky): same as the 100m to 80m, then the 4 x 100 fly zone
protocols.protocol: A race-modelling template rather than a conditioning session: the 200m is the 100m model held together through the second hundred. The 100m is executed as a sequence of holds each paired with a specific technical cue, separated by 5m breathing zones where the athlete inhales and transitions to the next cue. The 200m adds nothing new until 80m; from there the athlete enters the '4 x 100 fly zone', floats through the fly with a 4-in / 4-out breathing pattern, and holds posture with short ground contact times. Race modelling is described as 'playing a song with your body' — it supplies focus, order, rhythm, rest and a template for improvement. The drill vehicle is progressive hurdle-gate work: athletes in lanes 3 and 5, hurdle gates in lanes 2, 4 and 6, on acceleration or maximum-velocity days, with the coach cueing relentlessly through the later stages.

protocols.title: 200m race model (The Speed Project): four phases, curve mechanics and a 1-2% first-100 advantage
protocols.protocol: Four race phases mapped to energy systems: 0-50m ATP-PC dominance (explosive acceleration, max force first 10m); 50-110m energy-system transition while navigating the curve as anaerobic glycolysis begins; 110-170m lactate management as anaerobic lactic contribution peaks; 170-200m neuromuscular preservation as lactate degrades contraction quality. Curve mechanics: the prescribed cue is hip rotation aligned with lane angle with a VERTICAL torso — 'headlights following the road' — explicitly NOT lateral lean; the right arm crossing the body midline during a left curve assists rotational momentum. Curve force demands rise exponentially with velocity and tighter radius (Fc = mv2/r). Outside leg = forward propulsion (hamstring/ankle overload risk); inside leg = lateral force generation (hip/knee stress, longer ground contact). Phase 4 technique: powerful 'drum-beating' arm action to sustain leg frequency, maintain forward shoulder position, accept slight frequency reduction while preserving stride length, and avoid a premature finishing lean (final 2m only). Lane strategy: lanes 1-3 tighter curve, better competitor awareness — aggressive early pace to establish position before the curve; lanes 4-6 optimal radius, standard execution; lanes 7-8 wider radius, less awareness — execute your own race. Testing battery: 30m block start, flying 30m, standing triple jump, 150m time trial; plus monthly 300m time trial with immediate post-exercise lactate during preparation phases. Named mistakes: starting too fast, leaning into the curve, ignoring arm action when tired.

protocols.title: Speed reserve in the 400m and its race tactics: first 200m at 93-95% of 200m PB, second 200m 1.5-4.0s slower
protocols.protocol: Badon's model: pushing speed parameters on the low end (30m acceleration, 60m max velocity) raises mechanical efficiency at race distances, so improvements there give a long sprinter greater opportunity in the front end of the 400m. Because a faster athlete can run the opening 200m at a lower percentage of perceived effort than a slower athlete, the faster athlete typically cannot be caught even if the slower athlete has the stronger back half — 'pay me now, pay me later'. Race tactics follow: run the first 200m at 93-95% of the 200m PR, not at the PR. A developmental athlete will show a 3-5 second drop-off between the two 200m splits due to lower mechanical efficiency, and that gap should shrink with training and race modelling. Speed endurance is defined as the ability to endure/maintain max velocity (relevant to roughly 120m); specific endurance is the ability to carry speed through the straightaway and reduce late deceleration — the athlete should still 'look like a sprinter' with 50m to go, and being good at one does not guarantee the other. The 300m is used as a diagnostic: two athletes with similar 300m times can differ markedly in special endurance if one is spent and the other recovers quickly. Winckler's projection table (women) shows the mechanism: block 30m 4.35 -> 4.25 and fly 30m 3.30 -> 3.20 projects 200m 23.97 -> 23.33, first 200m 25.17 -> 24.53, second 200m 27.17 -> 26.53, and 400m 52.34 -> 51.06.

Second 200m = 1.5-4.0 seconds slower than the first. Average 400m pace is roughly 87% of the athlete's max velocity. Worked examples from the presentation: 200m PB 20.4 -> first 200m 21.4 (speed reserve 1.0s); 200m PB 25.4 -> first 200m 26.7 (speed reserve 1.3s); Merritt's 200m PB 19.98 with a 21.49 first 200m (speed reserve 1.51s) in the 2009 World Championships final.; rest_between_reps: n/a (race model); training implication is full recovery for the 30m/60m speed work that protects the reserve; rest_between_sets: n/a; weekly_frequency: Year-round emphasis on speed-related qualities ('dual track' training): acceleration / max velocity / speed endurance grouped together, with special endurance trained as a means to an end rather than the priority.

protocols.title: Elite 400m pacing: a sharp positive split is optimal (4-6% faster first 200m) — reported data
protocols.protocol: A race-model reference entry rather than a workout. The practical consequences stated: the last 100m of a 400m is limited by the ability to tolerate and buffer acidosis, not by top-end sprint speed (hence a 400m much slower than 100m pace x 4 is a lactate-tolerance problem, not a sprint-ability problem). Negative-splitting a 400m is almost impossible at elite level, and two runners with identical 400m times can have wildly different first-200m splits and felt effort — a 60s 400m run as 28.0/32.0 is a very different physiological test from 30.0/30.0. Reported benchmark context: 18-39 male intermediate-recreational 400m 1:12, high-level recreational 1:01, sub-elite 0:53, national class 0:50, elite 0:47 (world record 43.03); female equivalents 1:20 / 1:08 / 0:59 / 0:56 / 0:53 (world record 47.60).

protocols.title: John Smith (HSI) 7 x 100m rhythm workout at 400m race pace
protocols.protocol: Cones are placed at every 50m. The athlete runs 7 x 100m at 400m race pace, walking or jogging back only 50m between reps, so that the set carries the athlete one full lap and the whole sequence is completed in the order of turns and straights they will meet in the race — giving both visual and mental rehearsal of the 400m. The prescribed literacy is numeric: the athlete must know the exact per-100m target (12.25s for a 50s 400m). Variations are rep number (start at 4-5), recovery length, and rep distance (e.g. 150m). The session ends when times or mechanics fall away.

Worked example: for a 50s 400m (49s on the fly, allowing 1s for acceleration out of the blocks) each 100m must be covered in 12.25s on the fly. protocols.title: John Smith season sample workouts for 400m and for sprinters (Fall, Early, Mid/Late)
protocols.protocol: Smith's 400m programme is a long-rep, controlled-volume structure that mirrors the long-to-short approach: early season long repetitions with 12-15 minutes recovery (500m through 400m in 55s, 400m in 54s, 2 x 350m in 40.5-41.0s), a middle block built on 200s at 25-28s with only 3 minutes rest, and a late-season shift to short, sharp work — a single 350m in 39.5s, 200s in 25s, 10 x 50m. Wednesday's 300m rep at 40.5-42s with 5 minutes rest is the constant across all three phases, i.e. the 400m-specific anchor. The sprinter template runs in parallel: heavy fall volume at untimed/technique intensity (3 x 3 x 60m + 2 x 200m Monday, 10 x 100m walk-back Tuesday, 5 x 5 x 70m Wednesday, 8 x 150m at 60% Friday), an early-season power block (3 x 3 x 60m, 3 x 300m / 2 x 250m / 3 x 200m), and a mid-late season race-specific block (80-60-80-60 with 5 min rest, 4 x 4 x 100m). Start and relay work appears two to three times a week in the sprint template and Friday in the 400m template.
