protocols.title: Caffeine — dose and timing for sprint performance
protocols.protocol: Ingest 3-6 mg/kg body mass ~60 min before the race/heat; trial in training first; avoid within ~8 h of sleep.
protocols.dose: dose_mg_per_kg: 3-6 (minimal effective may be as low as 2); timing_min: 60 pre-exercise (chewing gum acts sooner than capsules); high_dose: 9 mg/kg not required and raises side-effect incidence; sprint_specific: some evidence that 5 mg/kg enhances single and multiple sprint performance (Astorino & Roberson 2010; Glaister 2008, via IJSNEM)
protocols.caveats: The ergogenic effect of caffeine on repeat-sprint ability is equivocal: one meta-analysis in female athletes found no effect, another found a benefit; 3 mg/kg failed in some female cohorts while 6-9 mg/kg worked (reviewed in the RSA meta-analysis). Inter-individual responder status (CYP1A2/ADORA2A) is not obtainable from published research — ask the athlete directly (see app_gaps).

protocols.title: Beta-alanine — carnosine buffering for the 400 m
protocols.protocol: 4-6 g/day, split into 1.6-2 g doses to limit paraesthesia, for at least 4 weeks (carnosine loading continues to ~10-12 weeks).
protocols.dose: dose_g_per_day: 4-6; carnosine_increase: up to +64% at 4 weeks, up to +80% at 10 weeks; responder_variation: high responders +55%, low responders +15% (Baguet et al., 4.8 g/day, 5-6 weeks); task_window: most pronounced effects in efforts under ~6 min (0-350 s); 400 m sits in that window; 400m_specific_finding: Derave et al. did NOT find a significant 400 m improvement (average sprint time 51.3 s); competition_role: benefit in highly trained sprinters likely lower; IJSNEM lists beta-alanine as more useful in training than competition for sprinters
protocols.caveats: Despite the physiological logic (400 m sits inside the <6 min buffering window) the strongest single 400 m trial cited in the position stand found no benefit; expect small effects in trained sprinters only. Paraesthesia is dose-dependent. Effectiveness cannot be verified without muscle carnosine measurement (not field-available).

protocols.title: Sodium bicarbonate — extracellular buffering for 400 m / 400 m hurdles
protocols.protocol: Single dose 0.3 g/kg, ingested 60-180 min before the race. Multi-day alternative: 0.1-0.2 g/kg at breakfast, lunch and dinner for 3-7 days (keeps the ergogenic effect, reduces race-day GI risk).
protocols.dose: optimal_single_dose_g_per_kg: 0.3; minimum_effective_g_per_kg: 0.2; higher_doses: 0.4-0.5 g/kg give no extra benefit and more side effects; window: 60-180 min pre-exercise; protocol_duration_multi_day: 3-7 days; event_fit: sprints of ~60 s duration — 400 m and 400 m hurdles; effect on shorter sprints unknown but likely smaller; mechanism: buffer against acid-base disturbance; also attenuated strength decline across a basketball game (Ansdell 2020)
protocols.caveats: GI distress is the main limiter and is individual — must be trialled in training, never first used on competition day. Acute fluid retention adds body mass, which matters for power-to-weight decisions. IJSNEM notes the competition-day caveat for sprinters (potential benefit vs GI risk).

protocols.title: Creatine monohydrate — dosing for a sprinter
protocols.protocol: Loading: ~0.3 g/kg/day (≈20 g/day) split into ~4 doses for 5-7 days, then maintenance 3-5 g/day. Low-dose alternative: 3 g/day for 28 days (slower saturation). Take with carbohydrate ± protein for better retention. Timing relative to a race is irrelevant once stores are saturated (4-6 weeks to return to baseline after stopping).
protocols.dose: loading_g_per_day: ~20 (0.3 g/kg/d) x 5-7 days; maintenance_g_per_day: 3-5 (large athletes up to 5-10); low_dose_route: 3 g/day x 28 days; washout_weeks: 4-6 weeks after stopping; sprint_role: aids rapid rephosphorylation of high-energy phosphates and shortens muscle relaxation time; likely greatest benefit in 100 m/200 m (IJSNEM); per-protocol_example: 0.3 g/kg/d x 5 d then 0.03 g/kg/d x 4 months in American football: fewer cramps, strains and total injuries than non-users (observational)
protocols.caveats: For a 400 m runner the trade-off is performance benefit vs added body mass and fluid retention — IJSNEM lists competition use as 'possibly' rather than clearly beneficial. Weight gain is real and matters at power-to-weight-sensitive body masses; individual response varies with baseline muscle creatine.

protocols.title: Dietary nitrate / beetroot juice — dose, timing and honest effect size
protocols.protocol: Acute: beetroot juice providing ~6.4-12.8 mmol nitrate, consumed 2-2.5 h before exercise. Short-term: up to 3 days of supplementation has also been used. Avoid antibacterial mouthwash around dosing (the oral-nitrate reduction step depends on oral bacteria).
protocols.dose: nitrate_dose_mmol: 6.4-26 across trials; intervention subgroup analyses used 6.4-12.8; timing: 2-2.5 h before testing; sprint_tests_used: 10-30 m sprints, repeated sprint ability (RSA), CMJ height/peak power, MVC, rate of torque development; competition_fit: IJSNEM: benefit possibly greatest in longer sprints (400 m, 400 m hurdles); 100/200 m possibly; evidence_quality: mixed — some trials show improved short-duration sprint power, others no difference or highly variable individual responses
protocols.caveats: Effects on short (high-intensity, non-endurance) efforts are inconsistent and the meta-analysis itself flags dose heterogeneity (6.4-12.8 mmol), outcome heterogeneity (CMJ vs power vs RTD) and under-representation of female participants — no sex-specific dosing guidelines exist. Individual responder status is not derivable from published data; trial it and record the athlete's own response.

protocols.title: Protein intake and energy availability for sprinters
protocols.protocol: Spread protein across the day: 0.25-0.40 g/kg body mass (or a 20-40 g dose of a high-quality source) every 3-4 h; total 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day. For a sprint athlete competing in a weight-sensitive sport, screen for low energy availability rather than prescribing energy restriction.
protocols.dose: daily_protein_g_per_kg: 1.4-2.0 (higher, >3.0 g/kg/d, studied for body-composition change in resistance-trained individuals); per_meal_g_per_kg: 0.25-0.40 (or 20-40 g absolute) every 3-4 h; sprint_context: ~0.4 g/kg high-biological-value protein every 3-5 h is the IJSNEM recommendation for sprinters around competition; glycogen_depletion: repeated 60-s sprints can reduce muscle glycogen by 70-80% (MacDougall 1977, cited); energy_availability_risk: sprint athletes may present with indicators of low energy availability (Sygo et al. 2018, cited)
protocols.caveats: Almost all protein-dose research is in resistance-trained or endurance athletes; sprint-specific dose-response studies are scarce. No published field measure of energy availability exists — the app needs the athlete's own intake, body mass and cycle data (see app_gaps).

protocols.title: Pre-competition fuelling and between-rounds recovery on a 200/400 m competition day
protocols.protocol: Pre-competition: a high-carbohydrate meal or snack providing 1-4 g/kg in the several hours before high-intensity exercise; a high-carbohydrate meal 4 h before exercise replenishes muscle and liver glycogen (Coyle et al., cited in the ISSN nutrient-timing stand). Between rounds: re-feed protein at ~0.4 g/kg high-biological-value every 3-5 h (sprint-specific guidance), keep fluids/electrolytes up, and expect relatively long recovery gaps; energy and macronutrient intake should be moderated relative to training days because competition energy expenditure is lower.
protocols.dose: pre_event_carbohydrate_g_per_kg: 1-4 in the hours before high-intensity exercise; pre_event_meal_timing_h: ~4 (high-CHO meal restores muscle and liver glycogen); between_rounds_protein_g_per_kg: ~0.4 every 3-5 h; between_rounds_reality: competitions are short with relatively long recovery periods between races, so total energy intake should drop vs training days to avoid unwanted weight gain; supplement_precaution: competition use of any ergogenic should be preceded by trialling in training to confirm tolerance
protocols.caveats: There is no sprint-specific, round-structured competition-day trial in the material fetched: the 1-4 g/kg figure is a general pre-exercise recommendation, and the 4 h pre-meal evidence comes from cycling. Specific gut-training protocols and individual tolerance are not obtainable from research — ask the athlete. No published protocol was found for the ≤2 h between-heats window in 200/400 m (unverified topic).

protocols.title: Competition anxiety / arousal regulation — 7-week mindfulness (MAIC) intervention protocol for sprinters
protocols.protocol: 7 weeks of systematic mindfulness-acceptance-insight-commitment (MAIC) training: group sessions integrated into the sprinter's normal preparation week (mindfulness level measured with the FFMQ; anxiety with the CSAI-2 at 3 time points). Control group received no mindfulness training. Broader preparatory-routine structure: pre-competitive activity routine (day before), pre-performance routine (immediately before execution), post-performance activity routine — combining relaxation, imagery, concentration and positive self-talk to reach optimal arousal.
protocols.dose: design: randomised controlled trial, 24 sprinters (M age 22.46 ± 1.35; 14 male, 10 female), recruited from high-competition-anxiety sprinters (CSAI-2 mean ≥3.5), 100 m competitors; intervention_duration_weeks: 7; outcomes: significant group × time effects for mindfulness (p = 0.027 and 0.028); reduced somatic state anxiety (SSA) and cognitive state anxiety (CSA); improved state self-efficacy/confidence; mechanism: mindfulness training targets mind-body experience rather than controlling or altering it
protocols.caveats: Small single-site sample of Chinese collegiate 100 m sprinters; not a 200/400 m sample and not blinded in the usual sense. Anxiety reduction is the measured outcome — the study does not demonstrate a race-time improvement, so the app should pair it with performance monitoring rather than promise seconds. Individual baseline CSAI-2/SCAT scores are required and are not in the literature.

protocols.title: Pre-performance routines — what the meta-analytic evidence supports
protocols.protocol: Athlete-specific, systematically rehearsed set of task-relevant thoughts and actions executed immediately before performance. Three tiers: pre-competitive activity routine (the day before — actions, thoughts, rituals that build readiness and confidence), pre-performance routine (immediately pre-execution, e.g. run-through sequence, trigger words, quiet eye), post-performance activity routine. Integrate into normal training rather than adding on top; modify according to competition demands.
protocols.dose: meta_analysis_scope: 112 effect sizes from pre-post and experimental designs, low-pressure and pressurised conditions; pre_post_effect: SMC* = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.44]; experimental_low_pressure: Hedges' g = 0.64, 95% CI [0.45, 0.83]; experimental_pressurised: Hedges' g = 0.70, 95% CI [0.24, 1.16]; moderator: effects were not moderated by type of PPR (extensive multi-element routines and specific stand-alone routines such as quiet eye both work)
protocols.caveats: Effects are small-to-moderate and heterogeneous (the pressurised-condition CI is wide, 0.24-1.16). 'Routine' in this literature is a psychological skill package, not a fixed warm-up script — the specific content must come from the individual athlete; there is no published 200 m/400 m routine protocol.

protocols.title: Flying 30 m test — protocol (60 m run, split at 30 m)
protocols.protocol: BrianMac version: 10-min warm-up; mark a 60 m straight (A–C) with a cone at 30 m (B); athlete sprints 60 m from a sprint start on the assistant's commands ('On your marks, set, GO'); assistant starts the watch on 'GO' and records the torso time at B (30 m) and C (60 m); flying 30 m time = C − B. Topend Sports version: cones at 0/30/60 m, timing gates at 30 m and 60 m; the 0–30 m zone is the acceleration zone, the timed zone is the 30–60 m; timing starts when the torso passes gate 1 (30 m); two trials, best time to 0.01 s. Start distance: 30 m standard; adjust the run-in for the athlete — 20–25 m for slower/developing athletes, 35–40 m for top-class sprinters who are still accelerating at the 30 m mark.
protocols.dose: standard_run_in_m: 30; run_in_range_m: 20-25 (developing) to 35-40 (elite); trials: 2; timing_gates_vs_hand_s: -0.05000000000000002; wind_limit_ms: 2.0
protocols.caveats: BrianMac times from the start command and subtracts (flying = 60 m time − 30 m time), whereas Topend times from the 30 m gate; the two are NOT interchangeable if the athlete is still accelerating through 30 m. Hand timing is ~0.15–0.20 s slower/faster than gates (see the timing_method_caveats field above and D-T06). The 0.15-0.20 s hand/gate figure is a coach-literature estimate, not a measured correction factor for this test.

protocols.title: Flying 30 m normative values (world-class table + 16–19 y UK table)
protocols.protocol: Same test as D-T01; compare best of 2 trials against the tables below. Record wind and surface with the result.
protocols.dose: chu_1996_world_class_male: excellent: <2.6 s; above_avg: 2.6-2.9; average: 2.9-3.1; below_avg: 3.1-3.3; poor: >3.3; chu_1996_world_class_female: excellent: <3.0 s; above_avg: 3.0-3.3; average: 3.3-3.5; below_avg: 3.5-3.7; poor: >3.7; topend_bands_s: elite: <2.8; advanced: 3.20; intermediate: 3.60; recreational: 4.20; velocity_calc: v = 30 / t (m/s); 3.00 s = 10.0 m/s = 36.0 km/h; interpretation_gate: sub-3.0 s flying 30 m ≈ 100 m under 11 s (Topend; needs sub-3.0 to break 11 s, ~3.2-3.4 for 12 s)
protocols.evidence_note: applied/secondary; the Chu (1996) table is a coach-textbook norm set, not a peer-reviewed normative study
protocols.caveats: Cartwright reproduces the Chu table verbatim and labels a second table (male <4 s / female <4.5 s) as a '30 m sprint test' for 16-19 y — that second table is the STANDING/block-start hand-timed 30 m, not the flying 30 m (BrianMac labels it Davis 2000, UK 16-19 y standards). Do not mix the two tables. Topend's bands are calculator tiers, not published normative data.

protocols.title: 30 m from a standing start or blocks, and the 60 m sprint test — protocols + 30 m normative values (hand time)
protocols.protocol: Topend: stationary start, one foot in front of the other, front foot on/behind the line, hold 2 s with no rocking; tester stands at the finish with one arm raised, calls 'ready' and sweeps the arm down to start the athlete (do not call 'go' — hearing delay); 2 trials, best time to 0.01 s, timing from first movement with a stopwatch, or from gate break with gates. BrianMac/Cartwright cue set: 10-min warm-up; 'On your marks, Set, Go'; stopwatch started on 'Go'; 3 × 30 m with 5-min recovery, fastest recorded. 60 m test (Topend Sports): same stationary start rules (front foot on the line, 2 s hold, no rocking; arm-sweep start cue); maximal sprint through the line, best of 2 trials to 0.01 s; can be run as 0-30 m / 30-60 m splits, in which case the 30-60 m split IS a flying 30 m (see D-T01).
protocols.dose: davis_2000_uk_16_19_male: excellent: <4.0; above_avg: 4.0-4.2; average: 4.3-4.4; below_avg: 4.5-4.6; poor: >4.6; davis_2000_uk_16_19_female: excellent: <4.5; above_avg: 4.5-4.6; average: 4.7-4.8; below_avg: 4.9-5.0; poor: >5.0; elite_reference: world-class sprinters are under ~3.70 s for 30 m from blocks (SpeedEndurance); start_type: blocks or standing; standing-start 30 m ≈ 1.0 s slower than the flying 30 m of the same athlete; sixty_m_splits: 0-30 m and 30-60 m gates double as the flying-30 m protocol; record wind, surface and footwear
protocols.evidence_note: applied/secondary (Davis 2000 textbook norms, quoted by both sites)
protocols.caveats: These are HAND-TIMED values; SpeedEndurance states explicitly the 4.0 s (male) / 4.5 s (female) 'excellent' standard is a hand time from the runner's first movement. Add ~0.15–0.24 s for equivalent electronic times, so never compare a gate-timed 30 m to this table. Cartwright's instruction to start the watch when the athlete reaches the 30 m mark and stop at 60 m is a flying-30 instruction mislabelled as a 30 m test — use BrianMac/Topend for the standing 30 m instead.

protocols.title: Conversion rule: flying 30 m time → 100 m time (Dick/Frank Dick controls)
protocols.protocol: Run the flying 30 m (D-T01), then read the predicted 100 m off the table. BrianMac also implements the Dick (1987) control-table calculator: enter the 30 m split and the 60 m time to get predicted 60 m / 100 m / 200 m; enter the flying 30 m to get 60 m and 100 m.
protocols.evidence_note: applied/secondary (Frank Dick, Sprints and Relays, 5th ed., BAAB, 1987, p.22-23)
protocols.caveats: SpeedEndurance's own conclusion: 'these control tests are simply control tests. The best way to determine a 100 m time is by running a 100 m.' The table is a coach control chart; it has no published validation statistics, and its accuracy for a given athlete should be checked against a real 100 m.

protocols.title: 400 m control battery: 150 m / 300 m / 600 m control tests, the 150 m endurance test, and the LAST test (500 m TT vs 50/100/150/200 m sum)
protocols.protocol: 400 m track, cones, stopwatch, assistant. 10-min warm-up. Sprint 150 m all-out (torso time), 15-min recovery; 300 m all-out, 15-min recovery; 600 m all-out. Feed the three times into the calculator to get a Speed Endurance Index and a Strength & General Endurance Index; the same page inverts the calculator to predict each control time from a target 400 m time. Companion test (BrianMac 150 m endurance test): one all-out 150 m from a standing start, watch started on first foot strike, stop when the torso crosses the line; used to predict 100 m and vice-versa.
protocols.dose: sprint_distances_m: 150 | 300 | 600; recovery_between_min: 15; reference_controls: Dick (1987) table of controls for 100/200/400 m athletes; published_norms: none located for this test; index_rule: Speed Endurance Index above target (with a 150 m time on target) = more lactic/speed-endurance work indicated; Strength & General Endurance Index above target = more aerobic work indicated; LAST_threshold_s: 5; LAST_source: Archer, L. (2004) LAST - Speed endurance assessment for 400m athletes, Brian Mackenzie's Successful Coaching, 16, p.10
protocols.evidence_note: applied/secondary; the source states 'I have been unable to locate any normative data for this test'
protocols.caveats: No absolute normative table exists — assessment is relative to the athlete's own previous results and to the target derived from their goal 400 m time. 150 m and 300 m control targets are generated by an unpublished Dick (1987) index, not by a fitted model. Numbers for the index formula itself are not extractable from the page (calculator is a downloadable spreadsheet). The LAST test's 5 s cut-off has no published validation or sample size (athlete count is a coach's self-report); use it as a training-direction flag only. 200 m split-run sessions should be logged as splits of the athlete's own 400 m, since no published split-200 prescription exists in the sources fetched.

protocols.title: Predicting 400 m from 200 m (and 100 m) — the equations coaches actually use
protocols.protocol: Run a legal 200 m (season best) and/or a 100 m time trial; apply the rules below and cross-check against the athlete's actual 400 m splits.
protocols.dose: mike_smith_rule: 400 m ≈ (200 m time × 2) + 10% — Mike Smith (coach of Roger Black); BrianMac's page implements this as the primary 200 m → 400 m predictor; one_hundred_m_model: first 200 m at 95% of 100 m speed and second 200 m at 87.5% for a well-conditioned athlete (BrianMac's optimal-pace prediction); elite_split_percentages_of_400m_time: 0-100m: 25.4%; 100-200m: 23.3%; 200-300m: 24.4%; 300-400m: 26.9%; elite_split_deltas: fastest 100 m is the 2nd; last 100 m ≈ 0.7 s slower than the first; 3rd 100 m ≈ 0.5 s slower than the 2nd; second 200 m ≈ 1.2 s slower than the first; worked_example: 100 m in 11.0 s → 95% pace for first 200 m (23.1 s) + 87.5% for second 200 m (24.8 s) ≈ 47.9 s 400 m; the 1.7 s 200 m differential sits inside the 1.5-2.0 s range seen in all good 400 m performances; energy_model: first 50 m from ATP-PCr; next 150 m anaerobic glycolysis with lactate accumulation; anaerobic systems engage at ~75% of 100 m pace (aerobic threshold); race_rule_of_thumb: 400 m ≈ 300 m time trial + ~1.5-2 s per remaining 100 m held at 85-90% of 100 m speed — see caveat (no single published 300 m→400 m equation was found; the 300 m control in D-T07 is the coach-supported route)
protocols.evidence_note: applied/secondary (Mike Smith, cited via Smith 1994 and BrianMac; split data from the 1988 Olympic 400 m final and 1993 World Championships)
protocols.caveats: Mike Smith's doubling + 10% is a coaching rule with no published validation; BrianMac presents it alongside (not against) the 95%/87.5% pace model, and the two will disagree for a given athlete. The 1988/1993 split percentages are descriptive of elites and assume lane-1-equivalent measurement. For a 300 m time trial to 400 m, no published equation with validation was located — the task's suggested '300 m TT' route should be treated as a coach convention, and the app should fit its own regression on the athlete's own history.

protocols.title: 400 m pacing evidence: positive split is optimal (Reardon toy model)
protocols.protocol: Not a test — the analytic result to encode next to any 400 m plan: first 200 m faster than the second is the optimal strategy, and the optimal strategy is to run at maximum propulsive force in the first 1-2 s then hold, for races longer than the critical distance.
protocols.dose: critical_distance_m: 291; above_291_m: run max force for 1-2 s then constant speed (Keller model); 400m_reality: maximum speed reached early, then continuous deceleration; ~20% velocity decrement over the latter three-quarters of the race; mj_wr_43_18: 200 m split data reproduce the model; predicted_negative_split: 100 m and 200 m runners negative-split (due to inertia at the start), 400 m and 800 m positive-split; author: Reardon, Am. J. Phys. 81(6):428-435 (2013); arXiv:1204.0313
protocols.evidence_note: peer-reviewed (Am. J. Phys.) + USATF course material
protocols.caveats: A toy model, not a fitted athlete-specific predictor; the paper's own claim is that positive splitting is robust to the accumulation function, not that it gives a precise target split for an individual. USATF's course notes the same 'start fast, minimise deceleration' strategy (Reardon 2013) but no closed-form per-athlete equation.

protocols.title: Strength/power and hamstring monitoring in the testing battery (CMJ, squat 1RM, Nordic break-point)
protocols.protocol: CMJ (Bosco/Ergo Jump style): from standing, counter-move and jump maximally on a timing mat; jump height from flight time via h = ½g(t/2)². Squat 1RM: general repetition-max protocol — warm up, 3-8 reps at a weight that is hard but technically clean, estimate 1RM with Epley/Brzycki/Lander etc. (±5% in trained athletes when 3-8 reps are used), or perform a direct 1RM with progressive loading. Nordic hamstring: standardised partner-held eccentric (warm-up 5 submaximal eccentric-concentric at ~50% and 5 submaximal eccentric at ~80%, then maximal eccentric-concentric reps), or a device-based break-point/force test.
protocols.dose: cmj_flight_time_bands_s: beginner: 0.4; average: 0.5; good: 0.6; excellent: 0.7; cmj_formula: h = ½g(t/2)²; squat_1rm_estimation: most accurate from 3-8 reps; ±5% for trained athletes; 7 validated formulas; nordic_test_reliability: ICC: 0.95; CI: 0.87-0.98; CV_pct: 3.54; intervention: 10 weeks of NHE; 1 set of 5 reps once per week → ~22% improvement in NHE test performance; nordic_protocol_waiver: some elite athletes can complete a full eccentric-concentric NHE with no break point; NHE halves hamstring injury risk (per the source's cited evidence)
protocols.evidence_note: mixed: applied calculators (CMJ, 1RM) + peer-reviewed reliability study (Nordic device)
protocols.caveats: CMJ flight-time bands are calculator tiers, not a normative dataset — no validated cm-by-age-by-sex norm table was extractable from the sources fetched, so 'numbers not extractable' for CMJ norms; store the athlete's own baseline and z-score within their own history instead. The Nordic device ICC/CV come from one reliability study in female football players — the values may not transfer to sprinters. Nordic hamstring norms (break angle/force in N or N/kg) were not extractable from the fetched sources.

protocols.title: Taper for speed-power events — duration, volume cut, intensity kept high
protocols.protocol: Reduce load by cutting VOLUME, not intensity: sprints stay maximal. Progressive (not step) tapers are generally preferred. Use a 3-5 day taper after low prior load, up to ~3 weeks after a heavy block. Pickering's own 2011 Worlds taper: day −10 4×50 m blocks + heavy weights (last heavy session), −7 3×120 m maximal, −6 low-volume high-intensity weights, −4 and −2 relay changeovers at max, −1 warm-up only, race day 0. Ben Johnson 1987: 4×30 m blocks and 80-150 m high intensity across days −10 to −3 with tempo days and two rest days.
protocols.dose: optimal_volume_reduction_pct: 41-60% (meta-analysis of 27 taper studies); taper_duration_examples: 15 days (35.7% of elite sprint coaches), 10 days (21.4%), 30 days (21.4%) — Agudo-Ortega et al. 2024; expected_benefit: ~3% (range 0.5-6%) competition performance improvement with a well-executed taper (Mujika 2012; Bosquet 2007); strength_taper_vs_rest: +2% strength with a taper vs -9% with complete rest; examples: Pickering 2011 World Champs taper; Ben Johnson pre-1987 Canadian Championships taper; fatigue_recovery_windows: neuromuscular 24-72 h; metabolic 12-48 h; structural 48-96 h; CNS/hormonal 72-120 h (Taylor 2016, cited); school_example: high-school sprint taper: TUT cut to 45 s (−56%), then −75%, then −93%; championship weeks to 21%, 5 s and 3.5 s TUT
protocols.caveats: Most taper research is in endurance athletes; the transfer to sprinting is inferred. The 41-60% volume-reduction figure comes from the endurance meta-analysis. Individual taper length varies widely (10-30 days) — the app must fit this from the athlete's own history, not assume a value.

protocols.title: The 40-second rule: what rep distance actually creates lactate stress
protocols.protocol: A hard run of approximately 40 seconds is required to incur significant lactic acid build-up. Therefore the ideal rep distance is 300m for women and 350m for men, because most quality 400m runners cover that in slightly over 40s - working a couple of seconds into lactate build-up while still allowing several reps per session.
protocols.dose: rep_distance_women_m: 300; rep_distance_men_m: 350; mechanism: >40s of hard running required for significant lactate build-up; reps_per_session: several (typically 3-4 for 300m, 3x350m)

dose_raw.mechanism: >40s of hard running required for significant lactate build-up

protocols.app_rule: For 400m athletes, set race-specific reps at 300m (female) / 350m (male) so each rep runs just past 40s; do not use 150-200m reps as the primary lactate-tolerance stimulus.
protocols.caveats: Coach rule of thumb consistent with the anaerobic-glycolysis literature but not itself a controlled finding; individual athletes may have different times-to-lactate.

protocols.title: Aerobic contribution to 400m racing vs training
protocols.protocol: The 400m only requires roughly 5% aerobic contribution to the race itself, but Hart still prescribes a substantial aerobic base (traditionally about 10% of training focus; in Hart's updated view aerobic training can be as much as 40%) to accelerate recovery between reps and allow greater total work. Endurance running is set at 100% emphasis in the fall and collapses to 5% in the late season.
protocols.dose: race_aerobic_contribution_pct: 5; training_aerobic_share_pct: 10 (traditional) to 40 (Hart's approach); endurance_running_emphasis: 100% fall / 20% early / 10% mid / 5% late
protocols.app_rule: Justify the aerobic block in a 400m plan as a work-capacity and recovery tool, not as race-specific work: heavy aerobic emphasis in the base phase, tapering to minimal by the championship phase.
protocols.caveats: The 5% race figure varies by athlete and by source (some put aerobic contribution to a 400m nearer 15-20%); treat as an order-of-magnitude statement.

protocols.title: Competition-phase weekly templates with exact paces
protocols.protocol: EARLY (Jan-Feb): Mon 2x500m @56s per 400m / 15 min; 3x200m @30-29-28 / 3 min; 8x10s rope jumps. Tue 8x200m @28s / 3 min; 6x150m long hills. Wed 4x300m event @42s / 5 min; 3x200m @30-29-28 / 3 min. Thu 1x350m fast / 15 min; 4x200m @26s / 5 min; weights. Fri 3x200m @30-29-28 / 3 min + relay hand-offs. Sat meet. MID (Mar-Apr): Mon 2x450m @52s per 400m / 15 min; 3x200m @28-27-26 / 3 min. Tue 6x200m @26s / 3 min; 5x20s rope runs. Wed 4x300m event @42s / 5 min; 8x100m short hills. Thu 3x200m @26-25-24 / walk 200m; 3x150m build-ups; weights. LATE (May-Jun): Mon 1x450m @50s per 400m / 15 min; 3x200m @26-25-24 / walk 200m. Tue 4x300m @42s / 5 min; 4x200m @28-27-26-25 / 3 min; weights. Wed 1x320m quality / 15 min; 3x200m @26-25-24 / walk 200m; 8x80m short hills. Thu 3 sets of speed-makers (50m all-out, 50m swing-down, 50m slow jog, repeat to 4 all-out sprints; 3 min between sets); weights. Fri 2x200m @26s / walk 200m + relay hand-offs; Sat meet.
protocols.dose: rep_distances_m: 200 | 300 | 320 | 350 | 450 | 500; rep_paces: 200m reps progress from 30s to 24s; 300m event runs fixed at 42s; 450m from 52s to 50s through 400m; rest_between_reps: 3 min for 200-300m reps, 5 min for 4x300m, walk-back for late-season 200s, 15 min for single long reps

dose_raw.rep_paces: 200m reps progress from 30s to 24s; 300m event runs fixed at 42s; 450m from 52s to 50s through 400m
dose_raw.rest_between_reps: 3 min for 200-300m reps, 5 min for 4x300m, walk-back for late-season 200s, 15 min for single long reps

protocols.rest_ratio: late-season 200m reps with walk-200m recovery (about 1:2.5-1:3); 300m sets about 1:7; single 450m/320m quality reps about 1:20+
protocols.app_rule: Progress the 400m week as: long overdistance with 15 min rest (early) -> 450m with 15 min rest and 200m reps at 3 min (mid) -> single 320-450m quality run + 200m reps with walk-back recovery (late). Weekly meet on Saturday, Friday is a light 2x200m + hand-offs.
protocols.caveats: All paces are for a 46s quarter-miler; frequency of meets assumed once weekly.

protocols.title: Season emphasis distribution across eight session types
protocols.protocol: Percentage-of-emphasis chart by training segment (Fall / Early / Mid / Late): Speed Endurance 75/90/100/100; Tempo Endurance 100/100/100/75; Strength Endurance 100/90/80/70; Endurance Running 100/20/10/5; Power Speed 20/60/70/80; Event Runs 25/90/100/100; Strength 100/100/100/100.
protocols.dose: unit: % emphasis per session type per season segment; segments: Fall (Sep-Dec) | Early (Jan-Feb) | Mid (Mar-Apr) | Late (May-Jun)

dose_raw.unit: % emphasis per session type per season segment

protocols.app_rule: When generating a 400m annual plan, weight session types with this table and shift emphasis at phase boundaries rather than abruptly changing session types.
protocols.caveats: Hart's own table; percentages indicate relative use, not time or volume.

protocols.title: Off-season training week (Sep-Dec), paces for a 46s quarter-miler
protocols.protocol: Mon: 2x600m @60s per 400m / 15 min rest; 3x300m @50s / 1 min rest; 3x300m @40s / 5 min rest; weights. Tue: 10x200m @30s / 3 min rest; 6x150m long hills / jog back. Wed: 4x350m event run @48s / 10 min rest (50m fast, 150m relaxed float, 200m split 28s, 100m picked up, final 50m steady); 3x200m @30-29-28s / 3 min rest; weights. Thu: 600-400-200-400-600 @30s pace / 5 min rest; 6x100m strides / 1 min rest. Fri: 2-mile timed run + weights. Sat: 3 miles. Sun: 20 min fartlek.
protocols.dose: sessions_per_week: 6; key_session: 2x600m with 15 min rest; secondary: 3x300m and 4x350m event runs; weights: 3x per week
protocols.rest_ratio: speed endurance 1:15+ (600m:15 min); tempo 1:2; event runs 4x350m at 10 min rest
protocols.app_rule: Use as the off-season template for 400m athletes: 2 over-distance sessions (600/500m) with 15 min rest, 1 tempo day, 1 hill/strength-endurance day, 1 event-run day, weights 3x, weekend easy runs/fartlek.
protocols.caveats: Paces given for a 46.00s 400m athlete - scale by the athlete's own 400m PB and Hart's pace table.

protocols.title: Overload progression: shorten the distance at constant pace
protocols.protocol: Start with 2x600m run through 400m at a slow pace. Gradually lower the pace of the first 400m until the runner struggles to hold it, then reduce the distance to 500m and keep the same 400m pace. Continue until the working distance is 450m, ideally reached by mid-season and held to the end of the year. Before a major competition run a single rep rather than two.
protocols.dose: distances_m: 600 | 500 | 450; structure: 2 reps -> 2 reps -> 1 rep before major meets; pace: constant 400m pace, gradually lowered

dose_raw.structure: 2 reps -> 2 reps -> 1 rep before major meets

protocols.app_rule: Progression rule for 400m over-distance: keep pace constant, chop distance 600 -> 500 -> 450m when the athlete can no longer hold pace; in race week do 1 rep instead of 2.
protocols.caveats: Requires timed reps to know when pace can no longer be held.

protocols.title: Predict 400m potential from 200m personal best
protocols.protocol: Potential 400m time = (best open 200m time x 2) + 3.5s, for a 200m-type runner willing to train for the 400m. First 200m of the 400m should be run at (best open 200m + ~1.0s) for the outstanding/experienced 400m runner, and (best open 200m + ~2.0s) for the less experienced one.
protocols.dose: input: best open 200m time; output: predicted 400m potential; split_target: 200m split = open 200m PB + 1.0s (elite) / +2.0s (novice)
protocols.app_rule: Compute every 400m athlete's pace targets from 200m PB: predicted 400 = 2x200PB + 3.5s; target first-200 split = 200PB + 1.0s (advanced) or +2.0s (novice). Use these as the reference for every event-run workout.
protocols.caveats: Coach heuristic, not a validated regression; Hart states it applies to 200m-type athletes who commit to 400m training.

protocols.title: Race execution broken into four 100m segments
protocols.protocol: Cover the first 50m at near top speed, then relax the upper body while maintaining leg speed. 100-200m: paced to within ~1s of best open 200m (settle into rhythm, feel the competition). 200-300m: a controlled pick-up - increase arm action, drive and lift the knees to resume a sprinting action, so the athlete comes off the final curve even or ahead. Final 100m: stay relaxed, focus on technique and form, avoid tightening up and minimise deceleration.
protocols.dose: segments: 0-50m near top speed | 50-200m paced within 1s of 200m PB at 200m mark | 200-300m controlled pick-up | 300-400m relaxed technique, minimal deceleration

segments: 50-200m paced within 1s of 200m PB at 200m mark

protocols.app_rule: Race plan generator for 400m should output: 200m checkpoint target = 200m PB + 1s, an explicit controlled pick-up instruction for the 200-300m segment, and a technique/relaxation cue for the final 100m. Rehearse each segment in event runs with timed splits.
protocols.caveats: Consistent with the positive-split pattern observed in 400m world records; the 200-300m emphasis is Hart's coaching judgement.

protocols.title: Speed endurance volume rule with near-full recovery
protocols.protocol: Speed endurance = runs at high oxygen debt with definite lactic acid build-up. Repetition volume is set by multiplying race distance by 2.5 (for 400m: ~1000m total). Recovery is ~10 minutes (range 5-10 min) so quality is preserved. Set examples: 10x100m (5-10 min rest); 6x150m (5-10 min rest); 5x200m (10 min rest); 4x300m (10 min rest); 3x350m (10 min rest); 2x450m (10 min rest).
protocols.dose: total_volume_m: 1000; volume_rule: 2.5 x race distance; rep_distances_m: 100 | 150 | 200 | 300 | 350 | 450; rest_between_reps: 5-10 min (typically 10 min)

dose_raw.rest_between_reps: 5-10 min (typically 10 min)

protocols.rest_ratio: work:rest approx 1:10 to 1:30 (e.g. 300m in ~40s : 10 min rest)
protocols.app_rule: Build 400m speed-endurance sessions to ~2.5x race distance (approx 1000m) using reps of 100-450m with 5-10 min (default 10 min) recovery between reps. Never shorten rest below 5 min in this session type - the training goal is quality of the lactic system.
protocols.caveats: Hart's paces are written for a 46s quarter-miler; scale all times to the athlete.

protocols.title: Tempo endurance: aerobic support with short rest
protocols.protocol: Aerobic work at slower-than-race pace, emphasis on quantity not quality, rest kept short (typically 2-3 min). Examples: 8x200m with 2 min rest; 6x300m with 2 min rest; ladder 50-100-150-200-300-350m with walk-the-same-distance recovery.
protocols.dose: reps: 6-8; distances_m: 200 | 300; rest_between_reps: 2-3 min; ladder: 50-100-150-200-300-350m, walk back same distance

dose_raw.rest_between_reps: 2-3 min

protocols.app_rule: Include 1-2 aerobic tempo sessions per week (6-8 x 200-300m, 2-3 min rest, intentionally sub-maximal pace) in the base and early phases; taper it in the late/competition phase.
protocols.caveats: Volume and pace are unspecified on the card beyond the rep structure; set pace by effort/RPE and heart rate, not by time.

protocols.title: Where 200m races are decided: the 100-200m segment
protocols.protocol: Analysis of elite 200m race segments expressed as %ST (share of total race time) and %PR (segment time relative to the athlete's 100m personal best). Races under 20s show lower %ST and higher %PR in the second half than races of 20s or more; better 200m personal records correlate with better performance in the 100-200m segment. An intervention applying this: the athlete deliberately ran a more controlled first 100m (speed and %PR below the smallest worthwhile change thresholds from his own pre-intervention races) and then exceeded SWC thresholds for speed, step frequency, step length and %PR in the 100-200m segment, which improved his 200m personal record.
protocols.dose: segments: 0-100m controlled | 100-200m faster than 100 PB-derived expectation; metric: %PR = segment time relative to 100m PB; %ST = share of total race time

dose_raw.metric: %PR = segment time relative to 100m PB; %ST = share of total race time

protocols.app_rule: For 200m athletes, build race plans around a controlled first 100m and a stronger second 100m; measure and log both segments, and judge progress on the 100-200m split rather than the total time alone.
protocols.caveats: Part observational across elite races, part single-athlete intervention - not a trial; segment metrics need reliable timing (electronic, both 100m marks).

protocols.title: Why 400m records are run with positive splits - the optimal-pacing model
protocols.protocol: A physiological toy model of anaerobic glycolysis solved with the Euler-Lagrange equation gives an optimal pacing strategy of maximum acceleration followed by optimal deceleration. For any race distance beyond a critical distance Dc (calculated at approximately 291m), positive splitting is optimal; below Dc, negative splitting is optimal. All ratifiable 100m and 200m world records show negative splits; all one-lap (400m) records and almost all two-lap records show positive splits.
protocols.dose: critical_distance_m: 291; model_output: maximal acceleration then optimal deceleration; rule: >291m -> positive split optimal
protocols.app_rule: For 400m race plans, prescribe a positive-split template (first 200m at target pace or marginally faster, second 200m slower) and never an aggressive negative-split plan. For 200m, prescribe the opposite: second 100m faster than the first.
protocols.caveats: Physics/physiology model (Am. J. Phys.), not a controlled trial; assumes a single dominant anaerobic-glycolysis limitation and no tactical interference (lanes, drafting).

protocols.title: Speed endurance during a taper: keep the intensity, cut the volume
protocols.protocol: Two patterns from the literature: (1) a reduced-volume week (taper) that included 70s SET intervals five times; (2) SET performed every fourth day for a 40-day period while weekly training volume was cut by 30-40%, totalling 10 SET sessions of ten to twelve 30s sprints.
protocols.dose: pattern_1: reduced volume + 5 x 70s SET intervals; pattern_2: 10 SET sessions (10-12 x 30s) over 40 days, one every 4th day, weekly volume -30 to -40%

dose_raw.pattern_2: 10 SET sessions (10-12 x 30s) over 40 days, one every 4th day, weekly volume -30 to -40%

protocols.rest_ratio: not specified for pattern 1; SET sessions otherwise use long recovery for quality
protocols.app_rule: Taper rule for speed-endurance athletes: reduce weekly volume 30-40% but keep speed-endurance intensity present (e.g. one SET session every 3rd-4th day) - never taper by removing intensity.
protocols.caveats: Subjects were runners with high VO2max; the 'keep intensity, cut volume' principle is the transferable part, the exact sessions are distance-runner oriented.

protocols.title: Energy system contributions during maximal sprints
protocols.protocol: Quantitative substrate split for maximal efforts: in a maximal 6-second bout, anaerobic ATP production derives ~10% from net ATP degradation (adenylate kinase), ~50% from phosphocreatine (PCr) utilisation and ~40% from glycolysis. In a maximal 30-second bout these shift to ~1% net ATP degradation, ~29% PCr and ~70% glycolysis. When maximal bouts are repeated, total work falls and the glycolytic rate is lowered (low muscle pH) while the aerobic contribution rises progressively.
protocols.dose: bout_durations_s: 6 | 30; pfcr_share: 50% at 6s / 29% at 30s; glycolysis_share: 40% at 6s / 70% at 30s
protocols.app_rule: Use these shares to justify session selection: for a 200m athlete, prioritise 20-30s all-out work (glycolytic) plus max-velocity work for the PCr phase; for a 400m athlete add longer 40-60s repeats. Repeated-bout sessions shift toward aerobic contribution - count them as aerobic-support work, not as PCr training.
protocols.caveats: Shares are from maximal cycling/running studies cited in the review; individual values vary with training status and fibre type.

protocols.title: Direct SET-P vs SET-M comparison with 300m outcome
protocols.protocol: 8 weeks, 3 sessions/week: SET-P group did 10 x 30s all-out with 3.5 min active rest; SET-M group did ~8 x 20s all-out with 10s passive rest and the aim of being exhausted by the 8th-9th interval.
protocols.dose: SET-P: 10 x 30s all-out / 3.5 min active rest / 3x week / 8 weeks; SET-M: 8 x 20s all-out / 10s passive rest / 3x week / 8 weeks

dose_raw.SET-P: 10 x 30s all-out / 3.5 min active rest / 3x week / 8 weeks
dose_raw.SET-M: 8 x 20s all-out / 10s passive rest / 3x week / 8 weeks

protocols.app_rule: For 400m athletes, a short-rest maintenance block (8x20s all-out with 10s rest, 3x/week, up to 8 weeks) is a legitimate and possibly superior alternative to classic long-rest 30s repeats - include both types across a season rather than only long-rest work.
protocols.caveats: Subjects were trained males, not 300/400m specialists; 3x/week for 8 weeks is a substantial load that needs monitoring.

protocols.title: SET-production vs SET-maintenance: the two speed-endurance session families
protocols.protocol: Speed endurance training (SET) means intervals above the intensity eliciting VO2max (for most athletes that is >80% of exercise intensities). Two families: SET-PRODUCTION (SET-P) = repeated short intervals of 10-40s with relatively long recovery, e.g. 30s intervals with 3 min recovery, targeting high glycolytic ATP turnover and sprint quality. SET-MAINTENANCE (SET-M) = efforts of 5-120s with shorter recovery to deliberately develop fatigue across repeated bouts, e.g. 1 min work / 1 min recovery, targeting fatigue tolerance - the athlete should be exhausted by the 8th-9th interval.
protocols.dose: SET-P: 10-40s efforts, recovery long (e.g. 30s work : 3 min rest); SET-M: 5-120s efforts, recovery short (e.g. 60s work : 60s rest; or 20s work : 10s rest); intensity: above VO2max intensity (maximal to near-maximal)

dose_raw.SET-P: 10-40s efforts, recovery long (e.g. 30s work : 3 min rest)
dose_raw.SET-M: 5-120s efforts, recovery short (e.g. 60s work : 60s rest; or 20s work : 10s rest)

protocols.rest_ratio: SET-P about 1:6 (30s:3min); SET-M about 1:1 or narrower (60s:60s; 20s:10s)
protocols.app_rule: Tag every speed-endurance session in the app as SET-P (long rest, quality) or SET-M (short rest, fatigue tolerance) - never mix the two within one set, and schedule SET-M at least 48h from a max-velocity day.
protocols.caveats: Definitions come from the review's framing; the review's own studies are mostly team-sport and middle-distance populations rather than 200/400m specialists.

protocols.title: Runners: 8-12x30s all-out with 3 min rest, 3-4x/week, volume cut 64%
protocols.protocol: Runners performed 8-12 x 30s all-out sprints separated by 3 min rest, 3-4 times per week for 4 weeks, while weekly training volume was reduced by 64%.
protocols.dose: reps: 8-12; work: 30 s all-out; rest: 3 min; frequency: 3-4 per week; weeks: 4; volume_change: -64%
protocols.app_rule: For a mid/late-season 400m maintenance or pre-championship block: cut total volume sharply (assume up to ~60%) and add 8-12x30s all-out with 3 min rest, 3-4x per week for up to 4 weeks, keeping everything else easy.
protocols.caveats: Performance measured as a 30s sprint test, not a 400m race; 3-4 SET sessions/week is a very high frequency that suited a reduced-volume design.

protocols.title: Low-dose short-sprint SET: 6x5s with 15s rest
protocols.protocol: 5 weeks, 1-2 sessions/week (8 sessions total) of 1-3 sets of 6 x 5s maximal sprints with 15s rest between reps and 2 min between sets.
protocols.dose: sets: 1-3; reps: 6; work: 5 s maximal; intra-set_rest: 15 s; inter-set_rest: 2 min; frequency: 1-2 per week; weeks: 5
protocols.rest_ratio: 1:3 within set (5s:15s), sets separated by 2 min
protocols.app_rule: In congested competition weeks where a full speed-endurance session is impossible, substitute 2-3 sets of 6x5s sprints with 15s rest / 2 min between sets (1-2x/week) to hold 200m-specific qualities.
protocols.caveats: Subjects were 17-year-old football players; 2% 200m improvement is modest and the test was not a championship race.
